articles.title: Chuva forte provoca alagamentos em ruas de Petrópolis | G1
articles.standfirst: Defesa Civil registrou maior acumulado de chuva no Vale do Cuiabá, em Itaipava; não houve ocorrência com vítimas.
articles.summary: Defesa Civil registrou maior acumulado de chuva no Vale do Cuiabá, em Itaipava; não houve ocorrência com vítimas.
articles.body:
Uma forte chuva atingiu Petrópolis , na Região Serrana do Rio, na tarde desta quinta-feira (1º), e provocou alagamentos em ruas dos distritos de Nogueira e Itaipava.

Os pontos mais afetados foram a Estrada Philuvio Cerqueira, a Estrada do Calembe e a Estrada União e Indústria.

Segundo a Defesa Civil, o maior acumulado de chuva foi registrado na região do Buraco do Sapo, no Vale do Cuiabá, em Itaipava, com 43 milímetros em uma hora.

Apesar dos transtornos causados pelos alagamentos, nenhuma ocorrência com vítima havia sido registrada pela Defesa Civil até o fim da tarde.

Na Estrada do Calembe, em Nogueira, carros estacionados ficaram quase submersos e estabelecimentos comerciais foram invadidos pela água da chuva.

Já na Estrada União e Indústria, na região do Terminal Rodoviário de Itaipava, os alagamentos dificultaram a circulação de veículos.

A Defesa Civil orienta a população a acompanhar os alertas e comunicados do órgão. Os moradores também podem cadastrar o CEP enviando uma mensagem de texto para o número 40199 para receber avisos da Defesa Civil e da Prefeitura de Petrópolis.

Para as próximas horas, a previsão é de céu nublado, com chuva fraca a moderada.

Segundo a Defesa Civil, o maior acumulado de chuva foi registrado na região do Buraco do Sapo, no Vale do Cuiabá, em Itaipava, com 43 milímetros em uma hora. — Foto: Redes Sociais

articles.title: Dono aluga apartamento mobiliado e diz que objetos sumiram em Ribeirão | G1
articles.standfirst: TV e itens avaliados em R$ 5 mil foram levados de imóvel, segundo empresário. Câmeras de segurança registraram movimentação suspeita de quem estava com as chaves.
articles.summary: Empresário denuncia golpe do aluguel em Ribeirão Preto após furto de TV e itens de R$ 5 mil em imóvel mobiliado flagrado por câmeras de segurança.
articles.body:
Um empresário diz ter sido vítima de um golpe depois que objetos sumiram de um apartamento mobiliado dele alugado para duas mulheres em Ribeirão Preto (SP). Um boletim de ocorrência foi registrado.

Segundo o empresário Octávio Candido Pereira Neto, uma TV, uma churrasqueira, utensílios domésticos e até frascos de shampoo foram levados. O prejuízo estimado é de R$ 5 mil.

O prédio fica no Jardim Paulista, Zona Leste da cidade. Para alugar o imóvel, as inquilinas procuraram a imobiliária onde ele estava anunciado e assinaram um contrato de locação. Octavio suspeita que a documentação apresentada seja falsa.

“Apresentaram documentos legais, locatária com imóvel no nome, fiadora. São duas mulheres, um casal. A locatária é a número um, a fiadora é a número dois. As duas possuem imóveis no nome, com profissões e, até então, sem nenhuma desconfiança”, diz Octávio.

TV levada foi levada de apartamento mobiliado alugado em Ribeirão Preto, SP, diz dono — Foto: Tiago Aureliano/EPTV

Segundo o empresário, as suspeitas de que um crime poderia estar acontecendo começou quando vizinhos e o próprio síndico do prédio passaram a desconfiar do entra e sai de gente no apartamento.

“Em uma semana e meia de locação, carro somente entrava e saía à noite aqui, ou final de tarde, ou na madrugada. Foi isso que chamou a atenção dos vizinhos, que nos acionaram. Até que nós descobrimos que, no dia 29, foi subtraída a televisão. Foi a última visita deles. Foi feito contato, já sem sucesso.”

Imagens de câmeras de segurança da última terça-feira (29) mostram o momento em que um homem colocou uma TV no carro que estava no estacionamento.

Octávio acredita que as inquilinas alugaram o imóvel com planos de cometer o crime.

“Desde o princípio, eles estavam com pressa para retirar as chaves. Tanto é que nós falamos, assina primeiro o contrato e depois vem e retira a chave (...) A chave foi entregue no nome delas, apesar que foi um terceiro elemento que retirou a chave e assinou o nome dele (...) Então ele facilitou a entrada de outras pessoas para vir aqui e subtrair os itens do apartamento.”

Homem carrega TV de apartamento mobiliado alugado e coloca em carro em Ribeirão Preto, SP, diz dono — Foto: Reprodução/Câmeras de segurança

Em outras imagens, uma mulher apareceu carregando mais coisas com um homem que estava com uma mochila. Do lado de fora, outra câmera flagrou duas pessoas saindo com sacos na mão. As chaves do imóvel não ficaram nem dez dias com as inquilinas.

“Nós nos sentimos enganados, traídos e, assim, impotentes, né, porque não podemos fazer nada. A gente nem sabe se essas pessoas usam nomes verdadeiros”, diz o empresário.

À EPTV , afiliada da TV Globo, uma das inquilinas disse que o filho dela pegou a TV e não avisou a imobiliária. Segundo a mulher, ele pretende devolver o aparelho nos próximos dias. Ela também falou que não retirou os utensílios domésticos do apartamento.

articles.title: Datafolha: veja como está a disputa pelo governo de SP | G1
articles.standfirst: Pesquisa divulgada nesta quinta-feira (1º) foi encomendada pela Globo e pela Folha de S.Paulo. Margem de erro é de dois pontos percentuais.
articles.summary: Pesquisa divulgada nesta quinta-feira (1º) foi encomendada pela Globo e pela Folha de S.Paulo. Margem de erro é de dois pontos percentuais.
articles.body:
Pesquisa Datafolha divulgada nesta quinta-feira (1º) mostra o governador Tarcísio de Freitas ( Republicanos ), candidato à reeleição em São Paulo, com 50%, e Fernando Haddad ( PT ) com 33%.

Veja, a seguir, os números da pesquisa estimulada, em que o Datafolha mostra aos eleitores entrevistados os nomes dos candidatos:

Tarcísio de Freitas (Republicanos) - 50% (eram 50% em 24/9)

Para 75% dos eleitores ouvidos no levantamento, a escolha do candidato é definitiva (eram 71% em 24 de setembro). Outros 25% dizem que ainda podem mudar o voto até as eleições, em 4 de outubro (eram 29%).

Foram entrevistadas 1.610 pessoas entre os dias 28 e 30 de setembro. A margem de erro é de dois pontos percentuais, para mais ou para menos, e o nível de confiança é de 95%. O número de registro da pesquisa é SP-01367/2026.

O Datafolha divulgou também os votos válidos. Para chegar a esse número, o Datafolha exclui os votos em branco, nulos e os eleitores indecisos.

Veja como fica o cenário considerando apenas os votos válidos:

Tarcísio de Freitas (Republicanos) - 56% (eram 56% em 24/9)

Na pesquisa espontânea, em que o Datafollha não mostra os nomes dos candidatos aos entrevistados, 33% estão indecisos. Veja os números:

Tarcísio de Freitas (Republicanos) - 34% (eram 33% em 24/9)

Vota no PT/candidato do PT - 1% (era 1%)

O Datafolha mostra também o quanto os candidatos são conhecidos pelos eleitores e o quanto são rejeitados.

Fernando Haddad (PT) - 45% (eram 45% em 24/9)

Tarcísio de Freitas (Republicanos) - 29% (eram 29%)

Votaria em qualquer um/não rejeita nenhum - 4% (eram 3%)

Rejeita todos/não votaria em nenhum - 3% (eram 3%)

Em um possível cenário de segundo turno, Tarcísio vence Haddad.

Tarcísio de Freitas (Republicanos) - 55% (eram 55% em 24/9)

Não sabe o número do candidato: 45% (eram 52% em 24 de setembro)

Entre os eleitores de Fernando Haddad, 59% mencionaram o número corretamente (eram 60% em 24/9), 40% não sabem (eram 38%) e 1% citou o número errado (eram 2%).

Nos que votam em Tarcísio de Freitas, 45% responderam corretamente (eram 34% em 24/9) e 45% não sabem o número (eram 55%). Outros 9% mencionaram o número errado (eram 11%).

articles.title: What’s driving Israeli settler violence in the occupied West Bank?
articles.summary: Attacks on Palestinians in the area are growing at unprecedented levels.
articles.body:
Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territory are illegal under international law, but Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government has approved plans to expand settlements in the occupied West Bank.

The expansion is taking place alongside unprecedented levels of anti-Palestinian pogroms carried out by Israelis from illegal settlements.

United Nations experts have said the rate of “settler terrorism” has increased over the last three years and reach a new peak this year.

The situation has eventually drawn harsh criticism from Israel’s allies in Europe.

But will that be enough to stop settler violence?

articles.title: Douglas Ruas: MPRJ investiga patrimônio de empresas do candidato | G1
articles.standfirst: A apuração começou depois de uma denúncia anônima apresentada ao Ministério Público.
articles.summary: A investigação do MPRJ sobre Douglas Ruas apura suspeitas de lavagem de dinheiro e peculato em empresas ligadas ao candidato ao governo do Rio de Janeiro.
articles.body:
O Ministério Público do Rio (MPRJ) abriu uma investigação a partir de uma denúncia contra o candidato ao governo do estado Douglas Ruas ( PL ). Os promotores apuram o crescimento patrimonial de empresas ligadas a ele.

A investigação do MPRJ que envolve Douglas Ruas, revelada pelo jornal O Globo , tramita em sigilo no Tribunal de Justiça do Rio (TJRJ).

O RJ2 teve acesso à portaria de instauração de Procedimento Investigatório Criminal, de 15 de julho deste ano.

O candidato ao governo do RJ Douglas Ruas (PL) — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo

O MPRJ apura o que classifica como um crescimento patrimonial e financeiro abrupto de empresas ligadas ao deputado estadual: a Saur Construção, Terraplanagem e Locação, uma construtora, e a DM Invest Consultoria e Participações, uma administradora financeira.

Segundo o documento, esse crescimento coincidiu com a ascensão política dele e de seu pai, Capitão Nelson, prefeito de São Gonçalo.

Ainda de acordo com o MPRJ, há suspeitas de organização criminosa, peculato, lavagem de dinheiro e crimes licitatórios . O órgão confirmou que Douglas Ruas tem vínculo societário com a Saur e a DM.

A apuração começou depois de uma denúncia anônima apresentada ao MPRJ. De acordo com o Ministério Público, foram reunidos elementos suficientes para a instauração de investigação formal.

Entre eles, informações sobre pessoas que estariam atuando na engrenagem criminosa noticiada, inclusive com a apuração de possível contratação fraudulenta.

Douglas Ruas, que é candidato ao governo do estado pelo PL, foi secretário estadual das Cidades do ex-governador Cláudio Castro.

Uma auditoria da atual gestão do Palácio Guanabara sobre contratos feitos na época em que Ruas comandava a secretaria também faz parte da investigação do Ministério Público.

A auditoria identificou contratos que somam R$ 702 milhões com consórcios liderados pela FP Vieira Engenharia.

Em um deles, a FP Vieira subcontratou a Mineração Santa Edwiges, da família do deputado federal Altineu Côrtes, presidente do PL no Rio.

O deputado federal Altineu Côrtes — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo

O Ministério Público afirma no documento que há uma ligação entre as famílias de Douglas Ruas e de Altineu Côrtes.

Um imóvel no município de São Gonçalo comprado pelas empresas Saur Construção, Terraplanagem e Locação e Normandia Empreendimentos e Participações seria outro elo.

A empresa Saur está no nome de Douglas Ruas e de Capitão Nelson. Segundo o MPRJ, as movimentações referentes a escrituras de compra e venda de imóveis da Saur, entre 2023 e 2025, somam o montante de mais de R$ 12 milhões.

Três deles, juntos, somam R$ 7,4 milhões. Dois estão localizados em Duque de Caxias, na Baixada Fluminense, e outro em São Gonçalo, na Região Metropolitana.

Ainda de acordo com o MP, esse imóvel em São Gonçalo da Saur aparece em sociedade com a empresa Normandia Empreendimentos e Participações, que pertence ao deputado federal Altineu Côrtes.

Além de presidente estadual do PL, ele é deputado federal e tem foro privilegiado.

Por isso, o caso foi remetido também à Procuradoria-Geral da República para avaliar se há existência ou não de fato atribuível ao deputado federal que justifique competência originária do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) para investigar na Suprema Corte.

“Os fatos mencionados foram entregues ao MP depois que eu fui anunciado como pré-candidato a governador, e eu confio no trabalho do MP. As informações chegam, eles vão fazer apuração, mas até o presente momento eu não fui notificado pra prestar quaisquer esclarecimentos”, disse Douglas Ruas.

“Recentemente, sobre os mesmos fatos, o MP arquivou um outro procedimento investigatório sem sequer pedir qualquer esclarecimento a mim porque verificou se tratar de fatos inverídicos. E tenho certeza de que esse outro procedimento aberto terá o mesmo desfecho. Em breve será arquivado porque vai se chegar à conclusão de que se trata de mentiras e ataques da velha política a minha candidatura a governador”, disse o candidato.

“Eu nunca respondi a nenhum processo criminal, tenho zero processos, nunca precisei contratar um advogado criminal pra responder por qualquer ato praticado à frente da gestão pública”, acrescentou.

Douglas Ruas — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo

A assessoria da Prefeitura de São Gonçalo afirmou que não responde demandas de cunho político ou pessoal do prefeito Capitão Nelson. O RJ2 pediu um posicionamento ao prefeito, mas não teve retorno.

O deputado Altineu Côrtes informou que a Mineradora Santa Edwiges nunca forneceu para a Secretaria das Cidades e para nenhum órgão público. Disse ainda que no mercado privado a mineradora pratica preços abaixo da tabela do Tribunal de Contas do Estado. Altineu informou ainda que o terreno foi adquirido por empresas privadas e antes do deputado Douglas Ruas ser secretário das Cidades e no local onde a secretaria não realizou nenhuma obra.

O RJ2 não teve resposta da empresa FP Vieira.

articles.title: Douglas Ruas promete expansão do Segurança Presente no Rio | G1
articles.standfirst: Candidato ao Governo do Rio de Janeiro pelo PL fez campanha no Mercadão de Madureira, na Zona Norte do Rio, nesta quinta-feira (1º).
articles.summary: Douglas Ruas visitou o Mercadão de Madureira e prometeu convocar aprovados em concursos policiais e investir R$ 1,6 bilhão em segurança pública no Rio.
articles.body:
O candidato ao governo do Rio de Janeiro pelo PL , Douglas Ruas , fez campanha no Mercadão de Madureira, na Zona Norte do Rio, nesta quinta-feira (1º).

Nas conversas com eleitores, Ruas falou sobre propostas de segurança pública para a região. Ele disse que pretende implementar o programa Segurança Presente para tornar a área menos vulnerável a roubos de rua e mais favorável aos negócios, "aquecendo a economia de um importante polo de comércio da Zona Norte da cidade".

"E u quero trazer para a Zona Norte, para todo o Rio, é o policiamento ostensivo frequente. O cidadão da Zona Norte, que mora nas comunidades, quer ter o mesmo direito de quem mora na orla da Zona Sul", comentou.

Ruas afirmou que, se for eleito, vai chamar os aprovados em concursos públicos das Polícias Civil, Militar, Penal e do Degase. Além disso, defendeu o aumento do número de PMs que atuam em todo o estado, com um investimento calculado em R$ 1,6 bilhão que, segundo ele, seria equivalente a 1% do orçamento do estado.

articles.title: Drumcree dispute: NI Secretary says 'no agreement' reached
articles.summary: Sir Chris Bryant spoke of his disappointment that the parties failed to reach agreement after more than two hours of talks at Hillsborough Castle
articles.body:
Agreement has not been reached on a resolution to the Drumcree parade dispute, Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant has said.

Members of Portadown Orange Order and the Garvaghy Road Residents' Coalition (GRRC) met Sir Chris at Hillsborough Castle for further talks on the Drumcree parading dispute on Thursday night.

Speaking afterwards Bryant told reporters: "I think this is the end of these conversations. We haven't come to a settled agreement, and it's a shame, but my door remains open."

On Tuesday, lawyers for the GRRC issued a fresh legal bid to try to prevent the march from going ahead. It was due to be heard on Friday but has been postponed until Monday.

Regarding the fresh legal bid by GRRC "we'll have to see how that plays out".

He added that "the law, in the end, is the law" and he would "urge everybody to cooperate with the police".

The chairman of the Garvaghy Road Residents Coalition said there had been no "meeting of minds" during Thursday's Drumcree parade talks and added that the current process is "done".

Breandán Mac Cionnaith was speaking after more than two hours of talks hosted by the Secretary of State at Hillsborough Castle.

Members of the Orange Order also held a separate meeting with Sir Chris Bryant and said their position on the march had not changed.

On Sunday, an Orange Order parade from Drumcree church did not take place due to a large protest on the mainly-nationalist Garvaghy Road .

Protesters have remained on the Garvaghy Road, although in much smaller numbers, and the Orange Order has maintained a presence at Drumcree Church, about a mile away.

The Orange Order delegation included Portadown district master Nigel Dawson and loyalist activist Jamie Bryson, who has been acting as their legal adviser. GRRC chairman Breandán Mac Cionnaith also attended.

Earlier, on Thursday evening, Mac Cionnaith said "the British government know what our position is," as the residents' group arrived at the castle gates.

"The Orange Order know what our position is," he added.

"I'm here to represent my community. That's all I have to say."

The Orange Order delegation made no comment to reporters as the group walked through the gates of the castle grounds.

Both the Orange Order and the GRRC were given a document during separate meetings with Secretary of State Sir Chris Bryant on Wednesday.

Earlier, Dawson said they were shown a discussion document in relation to the Drumcree dispute, but stressed it was "not a proposal".

The chairman of the residents' coalition said his group would agree to it, if the Orange Order did.

Dawson said on Thursday that the document shown to him "was very much an opening document and I read the document and there was nothing in it that moved the situation forward at all".

"And the document has now been removed from the table," he added.

Sir Chris has been involved in discussions with the Orange Order and Garvaghy Road residents since Monday.

It is understood that both parties on Wednesday signed a confidentiality agreement after being presented with a document from the government.

On Thursday, The Nolan Show revealed details of what was in the document that was presented to both sides in the dispute.

BBC News NI understands that it said the Orange Order had the legal right to walk along the Garvaghy Road; that the residents would accept that legal entitlement and publicly accept that it was wrong to block the Orange Order from walking down the Garvaghy Road - but in return the Orange Order would choose not to walk down the road.

Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) leader Gavin Robinson would not discuss the details of the proposal but told the Nolan Show that he supported the Orange Order's "determination and their dignity in the face of hostility and lawbreaking".

What is the Garvaghy Road dispute all about?

O'Neill returns to Garvaghy Road as police investigate Sunday's 'unlawful protest'

Drumcree negotiations are 'nowhere near dead' - NI secretary

Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) Chief Constable Jon Boutcher discussed the dispute at a public meeting of the Policing Board in Belfast on Thursday where he said the policing operation over the dispute has cost about £3m so far.

He described the situation as "challenging" - but said that despite "very significant tensions" there had been no violence.

The consequences of police forcing an Orange Order march down the Garvaghy Road "could be catastrophic" for Northern Ireland, Boutcher added.

During the meeting, it also emerged that the Policing Board has launched a code-of-conduct investigation into one of its members, Sinn Féin's Deirdre Hargey.

She was pictured taking part in an unlawful protest against the march on the Garvaghy Road on Sunday.

Sinn Féin First Minister Michelle O'Neill has been accused by the DUP of breaking the law by taking part in protest on Sunday.

In response, O'Neill said that if she was investigated then "so be it - that's the chief constable's job".

The Sinn Féin deputy leader returned to the Garvaghy Road on Wednesday to give further support to protesters.

Earlier on Thursday crowds gathered on the Garvaghy Road, including former Sinn Féin president Gerry Adams.

There were also performances by bands, including folk music group the Mary Wallopers.

The Orange Order, the most prominent of the loyal orders associated with Protestants in Northern Ireland, holds thousands of parades every year and the vast majority pass off without incident.

However, many Catholics see the marches as sectarian and object to them passing through, or close to, mainly Catholic or nationalist areas.

The Garvaghy Road had been part of the Drumcree parade route but by the mid 1990s nationalist residents protested against it.

Drumcree was one of Northern Ireland's most serious parading disputes, when stand-offs over attempts by the Orange Order to march along the Garvaghy Road were accompanied by riots, roadblocks and killings.

When the Orange Order was prevented by police from walking down the route in July 1995, there was a tense stand-off. It was the same for the next three years.

In 1998, the newly-established Parades Commission ruled that the Orange Order should not march down the road - a decision that was upheld for the past 28 years.

The row re-emerged last month after a court case in which a ruling by the Parades Commission was overturned, and a fresh application to parade was lodged.

Last Friday, the commission decided that the march could go ahead with restrictions in place.

articles.title: Twelve paintings hidden in a private collection for roughly 50 years are heading to a New York auction valued near $450 million, including a $180 million Van Gogh and a $120 million Cézanne
articles.summary: A collection of twelve impressionist and post-impressionist artworks valued at almost half a billion dollars is going up for auction on November 18, 2026,
articles.body: A collection of twelve impressionist and post-impressionist artworks valued at almost half a billion dollars is going up for auction on November 18, 2026, after sitting unseen for decades in a fabled private collection in South America. The paintings come from a collection amassed by the late Argentine art collector Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier and her sugar magnate husband, Carlos Pedro Blaquier, and are being sold by their children.They include van Gogh's landscape “Châtaigniers en fleurs” (Chestnut Trees in Flower) estimated at $180 million, and Cézanne’s portrait “Arlequin,” which carries an estimate of $120 million. Neither has been seen in public for half a century. Sotheby's auction house said on Wednesday that works by Vincent van Gogh and Paul Cézanne are expected to smash records for the artists in the sale to be held in New York.Helena Newman, Sotheby's head of impressionist and modern art, said the collection was like a “mini-Musée d’Orsay,” the Paris museum that holds one of the world’s greatest collections of Impressionist and post-Impressionist artworks. “In my 30-plus years at Sotheby’s, I’ve never had the privilege of handling a collection of quite this content and calibre,” she said.Newman said van Gogh's painting of flowering chestnut trees captures the "explosion of energy and vitality" the artist felt after his release from a psychiatric asylum in May 1890. Just two months later, he took his life. On the other hand, the Cézanne portrait is one of four paintings of the artist's son dressed as the Harlequin figure from clowning. The other three reside in major museums. Also in the collection are Parisian cityscapes by Claude Monet and Camille Pissarro, a horse-racing image by Edgar Degas and a boating scene by Pierre-Auguste Renoir, all valued in the tens of millions of dollars.According to art expert Philip Hook, a former Sotheby's auctioneer, the collection is "really the stuff of legend," because the collectors did not loan out the works for exhibitions. “No one really knew what was in it. So now, for this to be revealed, is tremendously exciting,” Hook said. “They came out with a collection that, rather cleverly, is focused on getting one representative work by each of the major names (of Impressionist and post-Impressionist art), and that is incredibly difficult to do,” he added. “They succeeded with huge, huge style and success.”Per Newman, the sale is likely to attract global attention, with potential buyers ranging from American tech billionaires to well-endowed Middle Eastern institutions and rich collectors from North America, Europe, the Middle East and Asia.“In times where there’s a lot of global macro geopolitical uncertainty, it’s almost like there’s a return to really established, tried and tested” works that are “unquestionably great,” Newman said. “(This) museum-quality Impressionist collection … is pretty rare.”You use AI every day. articles.title: Christa Pike's botched execution follows a pattern of issues with lethal drugs
articles.summary: Death row inmate Christa Pike survived her execution in Tennessee on Wednesday, reviving debate over a pattern of botched lethal injections in the United Sta...
articles.body:
Christa Pike , the only woman on Tennessee's death row, received two doses of a lethal drug in a Nashville execution chamber Wednesday night. But she didn't die.

Although her survival was "unparalleled," as one expert said, it was the latest example of a botched execution attempt involving lethal injections in Tennessee and elsewhere around the United States.

"All of this was predicted, and the court did nothing," said Steve Ferrell, an attorney for Pike, at a news conference Thursday, referencing the state's history of problems with its lethal drug protocol.

Pike, 50, was condemned for the 1995 murder of her former classmate Colleen Slemmer, then 19, whom she and two others tortured and killed in a manner widely described as gruesome, horrific and disturbing. Eighteen at the time of the attack and 20 at her sentencing, Pike was the youngest woman sent to death row in the country's modern capital punishment era.

The extent of Pike's injuries after the failed execution was unclear, but her attorneys said Thursday that she was still alive and receiving "lifesaving medical care" at a hospital. A doctor told CBS partner BBC News that Pike would have likely suffered traumatic brain injury.

Her legal team had said in an emergency motion to halt the execution Wednesday night that she had not lost consciousness, retained a heartbeat and could be heard audibly snoring on the gurney, despite correctional staff administering two syringes' worth of the drug pentobarbital to her through an IV. At one point, Associated Press reporter Kim Chandler, who witnessed the execution, said Pike "looked toward prison officials and asked if it was supposed to feel that way."

"The case of Christa Pike lays bare multiple reasons why the death penalty should be abolished," United Nations human rights chief Volker Turk said in a statement on Thursday. "The prolonged suffering — physical and mental — arising from multiple failed execution attempts is abhorrent, and cruel. And there are key fair trial questions still unresolved."

Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee, whose denial of Pike's clemency petition this week allowed the execution to move forward, has since announced the state will cancel the one remaining execution scheduled to take place this year, so that "a comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred" on Wednesday night could be conducted.

Pike's bungled injection wasn't a first for Tennessee. Earlier this year, in May, the state halted the planned execution of death row inmate Tony Carruthers when officers failed to establish an IV line through which to administer his lethal injection, after trying to do so for more than an hour.

At the time, Carruthers' attorney said he had been "tortured," telling CBS News that he groaned and bled from multiple attempted injection sites as staff tasked with handling the execution repeatedly punctured him in his chest, arms, feet and neck.

The defense team representing Carruthers had asked a Tennessee district court to stop the execution, alleging the ordeal "constituted cruel and unusual punishment," in violation of his constitutional rights, but the request was denied on the grounds that a burden of proof to demonstrate the state's actions were "cruel and unusual" hadn't been met.

Lee ultimately granted Carruthers a yearlong reprieve from execution, meaning that he'll return to the chamber a second time to be put to death after that. The governor said he wouldn't reconsider Carruthers' clemency petition, even as gaps in forensic evidence sparked public doubt over the legitimacy of the murder conviction for which he was sentenced to death.

Carruthers was among seven U.S. inmates whose executions by lethal injection failed because of issues establishing an IV line in the modern death penalty era, although researchers say other instances may exist. His attorneys' allegations of torture and unconstitutionally cruel punishment also echoed similar accusations from representatives of other inmates who've experienced botched execution attempts due to this problem.

In addition to Tennessee, these incidents have happened in Alabama, Arizona, Florida, Oklahoma and Texas, according to the Death Penalty Information Center, an organization that provides data on capital punishment but doesn't take a position on it.

Pike's survival was "singular and unparalleled," marking the first execution where an inmate remained alive after receiving lethal drugs, versus other instances where failure to locate a vein ultimately prevented the drugs from being administered, Robin Maher, the Death Penalty Information Center's executive director, told the AP. In a statement , her organization drew connections between Pike's execution and that of Clayton Lockett in Oklahoma in 2014, where Lockett appeared to survive the procedure but died of a heart attack while still in the execution chamber.

Tennessee resumed executions in 2025 after a three-year hiatus, triggered by controversy and criticism surrounding its execution protocol. Lee, in 2022, said the pause would allow for an investigation into its lethal injection process after it was determined that corrections officials didn't test the lethal drugs they'd planned to use for that year's execution of Oscar Smith for bacteria. That review led Tennessee to alter its lethal injection protocol, shifting from a procedure involving three different drugs to the current one used in Pike's case, consisting solely of pentobarbital.

The Tennessee Department of Correction said it "followed every step of the State's lawful, established execution protocol" in a statement released after Pike's procedure.

"The lethal injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective, and the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out this evening," the statement said.

Experts and groups advocating against the death penalty have sounded alarms for years about issues with lethal drugs used in executions. Declining support for capital punishment nationwide and skepticism over how executions were being carried out led pharmaceutical companies over the last decade or so to cut ties with state corrections departments, which, in turn, struggled to acquire lethal drugs.

Advocates have said this shift has contributed to increased incidents of lethal injections gone awry, accusing states of putting inmates to death with expired or untested chemicals. Because the details of execution protocols, within and outside of Tennessee, are frequently allowed to be kept secret , contesting them, legally, is difficult.

Pike's lawyers had raised concerns about Tennessee's protocol in appeals leading up to the execution, and Pike herself said she was "nervous" about how the procedure would play out in a letter that CBS News obtained from her spiritual adviser this week.

"I am not afraid to die. I'm only nervous about the process," said Pike in the letter, written Monday, before she learned Lee had denied her petition for clemency.

Her attorneys said the circumstances around Pike's execution proved their concerns had been valid.

"Tonight the State of Tennessee once again failed to carry out a lawful execution," they said in a statement. "We take no pleasure in being right, but the concerns raised by Ms. Pike proved to be true: difficult vein access, blown veins, degraded pentobarbital, no emergency medical care available when things inevitably go wrong, all under a protocol that remains veiled in secrecy."

articles.title: 92-year-old UK father changed his will while living with his daughter; wife was left with access to only half the money through her stepdaughter
articles.summary: The England & Wales High Court has ruled on the will of Mark Briant, a 92-year-old man who changed his will while living with his daughter and son-in-law
articles.body: The England & Wales High Court has ruled on the will of Mark Briant, a 92-year-old man who changed his will while living with his daughter and son-in-law in 2022. The change reduced his wife Rosemary’s inheritance to a life interest in half of his estate, leaving her without an automatic right to the capital itself. A later challenge argued that Briant had not understood the effect of the change. In a judgment dated 23 September 2026, the High Court found that he had not known and approved the relevant part of the will and removed the restriction on his wife’s inheritance.How did the 92-year-old father’s will change while living with his daughterMark Briant and Rosemary had been together for many years before marrying in 2011. Both had been married before and each had three children. They had made wills in 2012, but their circumstances changed considerably over the following decade.According to the High Court judgment in Elliott v Bateson & Anor, Briant had Parkinson’s disease and his physical health had deteriorated from 2017 onwards. Rosemary was diagnosed with dementia in May 2022. In early 2022, Briant suffered several falls and was unable to return home immediately because a suitable care package had not yet been arranged. He moved to live with his daughter Vanessa Bateson and her husband Ian in March 2022.A solicitor later visited the Batesons’ home on 11 May to discuss a new will and lasting powers of attorney. Briant’s new will was signed at the solicitor’s office on 20 May 2022. Rosemary and her son James were not aware that the new will had been made at the time.What did Briant originally intend for his wifeThe court found that Briant had initially wanted to leave Rosemary 50% of his estate. The other half was intended to go to Vanessa’s family. The estate was worth about £248,367 and consisted almost entirely of cash or similar assets.The important change came when solicitor Matthew Knight suggested that Rosemary’s 50% should be placed into a life interest trust. The idea was presented as a way of preventing the money from being available to a local authority if Rosemary later needed residential care.However, the arrangement did not give Rosemary an outright right to the capital. Instead, she was entitled to income from the trust, while Vanessa was to become the ultimate beneficiary of the capital. The court noted that Rosemary would effectively have needed Vanessa to agree to give her money from what would eventually become Vanessa’s inheritance.Legal Futures reported that Knight accepted during the case that there was no direct power in the trust allowing Rosemary to take capital from it. He also accepted that there was a strong conflict of interest because Vanessa was both a trustee and the eventual beneficiary.The change in will was not properly understood by BriantThe central issue was not whether Briant had the mental capacity to make a will. Instead, the court considered whether he knew and approved what the final document actually did.The judge found that the evidence did not show that the solicitor had properly explained the difference between an outright gift and the proposed trust. The court noted that the change had come from Knight rather than Briant. His original instruction was to give Rosemary 50% outright, allowing her to use the money as she wished.The High Court found that changing this into a trust was a fundamental alteration. Briant needed a clear explanation that Rosemary would no longer have an automatic right to the capital and that access to it could depend on Vanessa giving away part of her future inheritance.Legal Futures reported that Knight had not read the will over with Briant before it was signed. Although Knight pointed to a letter enclosing the draft, there was no record in his attendance notes showing that he had clearly explained that Vanessa would ultimately receive the capital.The judge’s decision about the disputed inheritanceThe court concluded that Briant had not known and approved the effect of the life interest trust on the balance of probabilities. The judge also found that the evidence about whether Briant had actually read the final will was weak and inconsistent.The court therefore removed the wording that created the life interest trust. This meant that the 50% gift to Rosemary became an outright gift instead of one restricted by the trust arrangement.The judgment did not find that the solicitor had deliberately tried to conceal the consequences. Instead, the judge said Knight appeared either to have assumed that Briant had a level of legal knowledge and experience that he did not possess or had not fully considered the consequences of the alteration.What happened to the claim of undue influenceThe family dispute also included an allegation that the 2022 will had been obtained through undue influence. The court rejected that claim.Rosemary had also brought a separate claim under the Inheritance Act 1975, arguing that the will did not provide reasonable financial support for her. Once the court removed the trust and restored the 50% gift as an outright inheritance, the judge decided that she had achieved everything available to her through that claim, so no additional award was made.You use AI every day. articles.title: Sexual assault charges dismissed against Trailer Park Boys actor
articles.summary: Actor Mike Smith had been charged with sexual assault in 2025 for an alleged incident in 2017.
articles.body:
A judge in Nova Scotia, Canada, has dismissed the sexual assault case against Trailer Park Boys actor Mike Smith.

The trial was set to begin in provincial court in Dartmouth on Thursday, but after the Crown provided no evidence against Smith, the actor's attorneys requested the case be dismissed.

The 54-year-old actor, who plays the character Bubbles on the Canadian sitcom, was charged last year for an alleged sexual assault in 2017.

Prosecutor Bryson McDonald told reporters outside court that the Crown offered no evidence in relation to the charge "based on the Crown's ongoing assessment that the prosecution standard has no longer been met".

McDonald would not go into further detail about the standard not being met or why, but said his office has been in regular communication with the complainant throughout the process.

There is a publication ban in place protecting the identity of the complainant.

The complainant said in a statement to Canadian broadcaster CBC that the trial was dismissed because she is "unwilling to sacrifice my mental health" by testifying.

Trailer Park Boys Incorporated, the company behind the show, said in a statement that because the charge against Smith was dropped, the actor will resume his responsibilities with the company.

Smith's attorney also said his client is "pleased that this matter is now behind him and is ready to move forward".

In February, Smith pleaded not guilty to one count of sexual assault.

Set in a fictional trailer park in the Canadian province of Nova Scotia, Trailer Park Boys follows the adventures of three longtime friends and petty criminals.

The Canadian mockumentary series first began airing in 2001 before ending in 2007, but was later revived by Netflix. Season 13 is expected to be released in the coming months.

articles.title: Syria denies officials held ‘secret’ talks with Hezbollah in Turkiye
articles.summary: Six sources from Syria, the US and Lebanon told Reuters news agency the reported meeting aimed to calm tensions.
articles.body:
Syria’s Ministry of Information has denied reports that government representatives have held direct talks with Hezbollah in Turkiye.

Reuters news agency said that Syrian officials and the Iran-aligned group met secretly in September. Reuters said they spoke to six sources, including two Syrian officials, a United States official and a senior Lebanese security source close to Hezbollah.

The ministry said on its official X account Thursday that the “claims are false. No such meeting took place”.

Turkiye, which reportedly brokered the meeting, also denied that it took place. The Turkish government labelled the claim as “baseless” in a statement on X on Thursday.

Tensions between Syria’s new leadership and Hezbollah run deep . The Iran-backed Lebanese political party fought for years to defend Bashar al-Assad’s regime, engaging in bloody clashes with al-Nusra Front , the insurgent faction formerly led by Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa .

The meeting was the first to be reported between the longtime foes and involved Hezbollah representatives, Syrian intelligence and Foreign Ministry officials.

Reuters said that sources spoke on condition of anonymity given the sensitivity of the meeting.

Reuters reported the meeting took place at the invitation of Turkish security and intelligence agencies in an effort to de-escalate regional tensions.

According to the news organisation, a Syrian official said both sides agreed they harboured no mutual hostility, with Syria assuring Hezbollah that it would not intervene militarily in Lebanon to disarm the group which is fighting Israel in southern Lebanon.

Syrian officials asked Hezbollah to help stop cross-border smuggling attempts and dismantle its remaining sleeper cells, particularly in southern Syria, the Syrian official said.

The reported meeting focused on resolving tensions between the two sides, and sources said it went well.

A Lebanese source told Reuters that contact between the two parties via Turkiye had begun about two months ago.

Reuters could not confirm where in Turkiye the September meeting was held, how long it lasted and whether other meetings had been held before or since.

Both Hezbollah and Syria’s government had signalled they would be open to discussions.

In July, Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani said Damascus was open to meeting the group. A month later, Hezbollah chief Naim Qassem said in a televised address that the group had no objection to meeting Syria’s leadership.

Three of the sources told Reuters it was Turkiye, a key ally of the Syrian president, that pushed for the meeting.

articles.title: Eritrea severs diplomatic ties with Ethiopia in tit-for-tat move
articles.summary: Ethiopia says it will shut its embassy in Asmara, declares 10 Eritrean diplomats persona non grata.
articles.body:
Eritrea says it is breaking diplomatic ties with its neighbour Ethiopia in response to the expulsion of diplomats from Addis Ababa, as fighting between Ethiopia’s federal forces and a coalition of armed opposition groups intensifies .

“Eritrea has no option but to reciprocate in kind and sever all diplomatic ties with Ethiopia with all the negative corollaries that this entails,” its Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement on X on Thursday.

This came shortly after Ethiopia announced it would close its embassy in Asmara “in response to Eritrea’s direct and indirect acts of hostility and belligerence against Ethiopia”.

Ethiopia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs also declared 10 Eritrean diplomats in Addis Ababa, including the charge d’affaires and others accredited to the African Union, “persona non grata for involvement in activities that pose a direct threat to Ethiopia’s national security”, requiring them to leave the country within 48 hours.

In its statement, Eritrea’s ministry said claims of its involvement in hostile activities were “astounding”.

“In reality, it is Ethiopia which has been pursuing an agenda of incessant hostility,” it said, adding that Addis Ababa had waged war against Eritrea to gain access to the Red Sea.

It also accused Ethiopia of hosting, training and arming Eritrean opposition groups to stoke internal conflict.

Addis Ababa has in turn accused Eritrea, ⁠Sudan and Egypt of supporting an opposition alliance led by the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) that has fought against troops loyal to Ethiopia’s federal government since last week.

Fierce clashes between Ethiopian federal forces and the armed opposition groups are continuing. On Wednesday and Thursday, explosions were heard in Addis Ababa, while fighters have also clashed with government forces in the northern Afar region .

Days after the latest clashes broke out last week, the chief administrator of the Afar region, Haji Awol ⁠Arba, told Al Jazeera that Eritrean soldiers had crossed into Afar to join the alliance’s offensive.

The fighting marks the biggest escalation since the end of a 2020-2022 civil war. Eritrea fought alongside the Ethiopian government during the Tigray war, but relations between the neighbours have since deteriorated.

Eritrea was not a party to the Pretoria Peace Agreement that ended the fighting in November 2022, and ⁠relations between the two nations quickly soured.

Ties between the neighbours have been historically fragile. In 1962, Ethiopia annexed Eritrea. An armed independence struggle, led by Eritrea’s current President Isaias Afwerki, secured independence in 1993.

When Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed came to power in 2018, he moved to end the tensions and normalise diplomatic relations with President Isaias. But Abiy’s ambitions to seek direct sea access for landlocked Ethiopia have contributed to tensions.

In recent years, Abiy has repeated that Ethiopia has a right to sea access, words that officials in Asmara take as a declaration of territorial conflict with Eritrea.

articles.body: Los Angeles mayoral candidate Nithya Raman hesitated while naming her favorite Los Angeles rappers during a Tuesday podcast interview, drawing laughter and teasing from the hosts weeks before voters decide whether she or incumbent Mayor Karen Bass will lead the nation's second-largest city. Appearing on the "Higher Learning" podcast, Raman was asked to list her three favorite L.A. rappers. She first named the late Nipsey Hussle and co-host Van Lathan immediately ribbed the city councilmember over her answer. "Wow. Look at you, media trained," Lathan said. Raman, 45, then said she still listened to "‘90s rap," but paused as she tried to continue her list. As the hosts laughed, Lathan told her, "And okay, as you search for the names, keep going." "I’m just shy," Raman said. SEE IT: LA DEM CANDIDATES TORCHED BY DISGUSTED RESIDENTS AFTER ‘DISGRACEFUL’ DEBATE: ‘BOTH BAD’ Raman eventually added Snoop Dogg and Tupac Shakur. Lathan summed up her list as "Nip, Pac, Snoop," while Raman explained that the music was what she listened to alone in her car and described it as "the songs of my youth." Lisa Cusack, President of the Don't L.A. My Burbank PAC, told Fox News Digital she believed the exchange undercut Raman’s efforts to portray herself as closely connected to Los Angeles culture. "Interesting that Raman called illegal street vendors an ‘indispensable part’ of L.A.'s culture, but can’t name some of the city’s most famous rappers. She later settled in Los Angeles and lives in Silver Lake, according to The Los Angeles Times. She was elected to the Los Angeles City Council in 2020 and currently represents the city's 4th district, including neighborhoods such as Hollywood, Sherman Oaks and Van Nuys. Los Angeles County Republican Party Chairwoman Roxanne Hoge used the exchange to criticize Raman over the city’s business climate. "I'd rather Raman be able to name her top three thriving L.A. businesses," Hoge said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "She can't." Raman narrowly secured the second runoff spot behind Bass after passing Republican candidate and TV personality Spencer Pratt during the extended vote count, after Pratt led Raman on election night. Raman has increasingly centered her campaign on dissatisfaction with City Hall's handling of homelessness, basic city services and the entertainment industry. "I came into this race because I feel passionately about the future of Los Angeles and I feel frustration about the current state of the city. And I think that a third of voters is out there feeling those same things," Raman said. Recently, Raman was pressed during a mayoral debate over her campaign’s decision to hire a consulting firm that previously worked with former Maine Senate candidate Graham Platner. A recent UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies poll found Raman leading Bass 39% to 28% among likely Los Angeles voters, while 33% remained undecided. articles.body: New York’s elimination of religious exemptions for school vaccine mandates is threatening to drive Amish families from the state, according to First Liberty Institute attorney Hiram Sasser, who is urging the Supreme Court to intervene in the ongoing legal battle. For decades, New York allowed religious exemptions for schoolchildren. But the state repealed that exemption in 2019, leaving Amish families and their small private schools facing vaccination requirements and potentially crippling fines. The 2nd Circuit upheld the law in June, and the Amish have since asked the Supreme Court to take up the case. "For decades, New York had a religious exemption for their vaccine mandate that they had on the books, and it protected the Amish who've been there for over 200 years," Sasser told Fox News Digital Wednesday. ‘COVID 2.0’: LAWMAKERS PUSH BACK ON SWEEPING HEALTH 'POLICE POWER' IN KEY BATTLEGROUND STATE "And it's just such a shame that New York is one of the only states in America that decided that they wanted to get rid of their vaccine religious exemption and to try to impose it on everybody, including private schools and, unfortunately, hitting the Amish who have their own ‘Little House on the Prairie’-style schools that they have on their farms," Sasser said. "And, for whatever reason, New York decided that they were going to start enforcing this requirement on the Amish who, frankly, just don't participate in these kinds of things. And instead of just leaving the Amish alone, New York decided to enforce it." Sasser said the state has put "crushing fines" on the Amish, which are endangering their farms and even the ability to stay in New York. CATHOLIC NUNS CARING FOR DYING PATIENTS FIGHT NEW YORK TRANS RULE, FACE JAIL TIME "We're representing the Amish, and I got to tell you, when they filed their declaration with the court, it was, it's handwritten because that's how they do it, and they work as a community together. … They want to be really good citizens. But they're holding the fort, so to speak, of a way of life that we all used to live," Sasser said. "Frankly, the Amish would just like to be left alone, but they still really want to be positive members of the community. articles.title: Most Americans say US-Israel war on Iran not worth fighting: Poll
articles.summary: Nearly 70 percent of Americans say the US-Israeli war is not worth fighting, marking a significant spike since July.
articles.body:
Approximately 70 percent of US adults in a new nationwide poll say the US-Israeli war has not been worth fighting, a five-point spike since July.

“Seventy-one percent of adults disapprove of how Trump is handling Iran and 69 percent say the war in Iran has not been worth fighting,” said the survey released on Thursday by The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research.

The poll, which surveyed more than 2,000 adults in the US, also suggested that Americans are deeply frustrated with US President Donald Trump’s handling of the economy and rising prices, with only 17 percent of US adults polled approving of his handling of the cost of living. Just 26 percent approved of his handling of the economy overall, marking a new low.

Public angst over fuel costs has surged, with about half of respondents now deeply concerned about being able to fill their tanks —up from 39 percent in July. Roughly half of respondents are also highly concerned about being able to afford food.

The data comes as Trump kickstarts his midterm campaign trail in an all-in effort to galvanise the Republican base, stumping first in Texas and Oklahoma amid widespread voter anxiety surrounding the war on Iran’s mounting economic fallout.

The poll also indicated that, despite their frustration, two-thirds of Republicans surveyed said that higher than usual prices are due to factors outside of Trump’s control, with about one-third saying it was directly related to Trump’s policies.

The sombre numbers suggest the president remains deeply unpopular nationally, with some Republicans also faulting him for failing to deliver on promised relief.

Overall, more than half of adult respondents said the national economy and the country as a whole are worse off since President Trump took office again in 2025.

In an interview with TIME magazine, published on Thursday, Trump was asked if the deeply unwanted war would threaten his party’s chances in November, to which he initially responded, “It’s possible,” before adding that “it should help, because Iran will not have a nuclear weapon.”

Confronted with sliding poll numbers, Trump said that the “pollsters are corrupt” and that the bad polls “are fake”, adding that he would beat anybody running today “by 20 points”.

articles.title: UK-Iranian dual national arrested in US airbase RAF Fairford incident, police say
articles.summary: British authorities on Thursday arrested a 27-year-old man with dual United Kingdom and Iranian nationality in connection to the thwarted alleged terrorist attack earlier this week on a U.S.-operated air base owned by the U.K. The man was arrested in the City of Westminster, London, “on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts” after British police looked…
articles.body:
British authorities on Thursday arrested a 27-year-old man with dual United Kingdom and Iranian nationality in connection to the thwarted alleged terrorist attack earlier this week on a U.S.-operated air base owned by the U.K.

The man was arrested in the City of Westminster, London, “on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts” after British police looked into suspicious activity outside RAF Fairford air base late Saturday night into early Sunday morning, according to U.K. counterterrorism police.

A second man, 26, who is a U.K. national, also has been questioned in relation to the incident, and police have searched two properties in London.

Authorities on Sunday initially arrested five men on explosives and terror charges near RAF Fairford — about 90 miles west of London in the county of Gloucestershire — after a local farmer called police over three suspicious vehicles and men wearing masks near the base late Saturday night. The men, all five of whom are British nationals in their 20s, were released on bail a day later.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Wednesday his government believes that Iran “played a part” in the incident.

“The investigation into circumstances surrounding events in Gloucestershire is hugely complex, and our specialist teams are interrogating multiple lines of enquiry,” Vicki Evans, senior national coordinator for the U.K.’s Counter Terrorism Policing, said of the latest arrest.

“As we’ve made clear, we’re looking at all possible angles — including possible foreign state involvement. I’d like to thank the public for their continued support and patience whilst we work through this investigation,” she added.

The U.S. has used RAF Fairford to position B-52 and B-1 bombers as part of the Trump administration’s war against Iran .

Tehran over the summer threatened that “any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces,” though it has denied it had anything to do with recent events at RAF Fairford.

The Iranian Embassy in the U.K. said in a Monday statement that it “categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations” regarding the Islamic Republic’s potential role in the incident.

articles.title: Nobody is working harder on room security, says Travelodge boss
articles.summary: A review found that guests are still not as safe as they should be in Travelodge hotels.
articles.body:
The interim chief executive of Travelodge has told the BBC "nobody is working harder on security of rooms in this industry than we are today".

It comes after a damning review found guests were still not as safe as they should be, with room intrusions reported at nearly one-in-10 Travelodge hotels this summer, and no policy in place on violence against women and girls.

Interim CEO Ray Reidy said the chain has made a "number of changes" since an attack at its Maidenhead hotel in December 2022 became national news earlier this year.

He said the woman was a victim of a "heinous crime", adding: "We are desperately sorry that she didn't get the protection that she deserved."

Kyran Smith, who obtained the key by falsely claiming to be the woman's boyfriend, was jailed for seven-and-a-half years in January.

The review found Smith was handed the key less than three minutes after approaching the reception desk, by a receptionist who had received no training in key security.

Barrister Paul Greaney KC, who carried out the review, said blame rested with Travelodge, that has its HQ in Thame, Oxfordshire, as an organisation rather than with individual staff, and a culture had developed in which room intrusions were regarded as "one of those things".

The woman emailed a complaint to Travelodge in January 2023, addressed to chief executive Jo Boydell and others.

The review concluded the email was handled by her office without her knowledge, and did not come to Boydell's attention until March 2026.

The woman's complaint was instead investigated by a manager who was himself criticised in it, and the customer services team offered her a refund for her night's stay, which she understood to be £30.

Reidy refused to say whether the victim has been offered any compensation.

The review said changes made this year had been done quickly "albeit years too late" and its new key security policy would prevent a repeat of the Maidenhead attack if applied correctly.

But it found the policy was "not being applied with anything like sufficient consistency on the ground".

It also found that mystery shoppers were able to get into rooms through housekeeping staff at all five hotels tested, including Maidenhead, without being sent to reception or asked for proof they were entitled to enter.

The review said the "results across the board were disturbing".

At three of the hotels, staff confirmed a guest was staying there, and at two, room numbers were said out loud at check-in. The Maidenhead hotel scored worst of the five.

Reidy, who was appointed intermin CEO in August after former boss Jo Boydell resigned - said training that has been implemented is "not an overnight fix".

"Training needs to be followed up with validation, it needs to be pressure tested in situ, and that's one of the reasons we are pushing out, extending the audit process, and also using the Mystery Shopper campaigns."

Joshua Reynolds, MP for Maidenhead, said: "It's a shame that three years has been lost between the incident and now, when things are actually starting to change to make sure that there are policies are in place and findings to make sure this has happened.

"What I want to now make sure of is that the report is implemented and that every recommendation in the report is taken on by Travelodge and fully implemented."

Reidy said: "We embrace all of the findings in the review, we accept the recommendations and we will address all of those."

Reidy said the company does not have a policy for violence against women and girls, but said it is working with the Suzy Lamplugh Trust - a personal safety charity - to develop one.

Greaney said room intrusions were a problem across the hotel sector.

Speaking on the safety of guests, Reidy said: "In rooms today you are safe, so we are confident in that.

"What we can't guarantee is that there aren't the room intrusions, so the review itself calls out the fact that when you've got an interaction between the customer and a colleague there is inevitably going to be an opportunity for human error in that process.

"Our job now is to try and minimise the opportunity for that human error and to make sure that we are making the rooms as safe as possible."

Reidy said while all hotels operate in the same way, the review found that additional training was required at Maidenhead.

"We have absolutely done that, and we've got our arms around that team specifically today because obviously the language in the report is quite damning," he added.

articles.title: In 2011, Stephen King and Tabitha’s foundation gave $120,000 to help heat Maine homes, as their radio fundraiser brought in $241,820 for residents facing a winter with reduced federal aid
articles.summary: In December 2011, international bestselling author Stephen King and his wife, Tabitha, helped Maine families facing a difficult winter by donating
articles.body: In December 2011, international bestselling author Stephen King and his wife, Tabitha, helped Maine families facing a difficult winter by donating $120,000 to a home-heating fundraiser organised through the author’s radio station. The campaign eventually raised $241,820, surpassing its original goal as residents confronted higher heating costs and reduced federal assistance. The Bangor Daily News reported that the Kings’ contribution came through the Stephen and Tabitha King Foundation, which has long supported community organisations and social causes in Maine. The fundraiser offered immediate help to people who might otherwise have had to choose between heating their homes, buying food and paying other essential bills during the state’s cold winter months. Read on to know more about it here:A winter of growing concernMaine winters can be harsh, and heating a home is a basic necessity rather than an optional expense. For households with low incomes, older residents and people facing unemployment or rising energy bills, a cold spell can create a financial emergency.In 2011, the pressure was intensified by concerns over reduced federal aid for heating assistance. Many Maine residents depended on programmes that helped cover the cost of fuel, electricity or other forms of home heating. When less funding was available, local charities and community groups were left trying to fill the gap. The need was especially urgent because people often cannot simply reduce heating without consequences. Turning down the heat can put children, older adults and people with health conditions at risk. It can also lead to frozen pipes and damage to homes during periods of severe cold.Against that background, the radio fundraiser gave listeners a direct way to respond. Instead of waiting for a long-term policy solution, the campaign focused on helping families meet an immediate need.A radio station turns to its listenersThe fundraiser was organised through the Kings’ radio station, which used its audience to draw attention to the shortage of heating assistance. The station appealed to listeners and community members for donations that could be distributed to Maine residents struggling to pay their winter heating bills. The campaign initially had a target, but donations quickly exceeded expectations. According to the Bangor Daily News report, the appeal eventually brought in $241,820, including the $120,000 donation from the Stephen and Tabitha King Foundation.The additional money was significant because it increased the number of households that could receive support. A campaign that began with one fundraising goal ended with an extra $100,000 raised, allowing local organisers to respond to more requests for assistance. Radio also gave the fundraiser a personal and immediate quality. Listeners could hear about the need, decide to contribute and watch the total rise as the campaign progressed. That sense of shared participation helped turn the appeal into a broader community effort.The Kings’ contributionStephen King and Tabitha King made their donation through the foundation they established to support charitable, educational and community causes. The foundation has contributed to organisations across Maine, including groups working in health, education, the arts and social services. Their $120,000 contribution provided a strong foundation for the campaign. It also drew attention to the scale of the need at a time when many Maine households were facing uncertainty about how they would keep their homes warm. The donation was not simply a symbolic gesture. Heating assistance can cover practical costs such as fuel deliveries, electric bills and emergency support when a household runs out of heating oil or cannot afford its next supply. For families receiving help, the money could mean maintaining a safe indoor temperature during freezing weather. It could also provide breathing room for households already struggling with rent, groceries, medical expenses and transportation costs.Why support for heating mattersHelp with home heating often goes to people who work but can’t afford a sudden energy bill. A small rise in fuel prices or an unexpected bill can tip a household into crisis. Older adults who stay at home more and may be at greater health risk in cold weather may be especially vulnerable. Families with young children also face difficult choices when heating costs rise, especially if they rely on a fixed or unpredictable income.Heating insecurity isn't just about being uncomfortable. Cold homes can worsen respiratory problems, and make people more vulnerable to illness. Families may use unsafe alternative methods to stay warm, while frozen pipes can cause costly damage to homes and rental properties. Community donations help organisations respond quickly. Unlike some government programmes, local funds can sometimes be distributed more flexibly when a family faces an immediate emergency.A wider community responseThe fundraiser’s final total showed that the campaign was not dependent on one major donor. The Kings’ foundation gave $120,000, but listeners and other supporters contributed enough to bring the total to $241,820. That collective effort reflected the way local fundraising can combine institutional support with individual donations. Some give big sums, some give small sums which become important when thousands of people give.The organizers were able to potentially support more households or make larger grants to those most in need, as raising more than double the initial additional target. It also showed how appeals to the general public could help to highlight issues that might otherwise go unnoticed. Many families do not publicly discuss their inability to pay for heating. A radio campaign helped make the issue visible without requiring each household to explain its circumstances publicly.The lasting meaning of the campaignThe 2011 fundraiser was rooted in a specific moment of financial pressure, but the need it addressed remains familiar. Every winter, households in cold-weather states must manage energy costs alongside food, housing, medical care and other essentials. Stephen and Tabitha King’s donation helped turn public concern into practical support. The final $241,820 raised through the radio campaign provided resources for residents who were facing a winter with less federal assistance and fewer options.The effort also showed how a community can respond when a basic need becomes difficult for many people to afford. A foundation’s major contribution, combined with donations from listeners, created a fund that could reach families before a heating crisis became a health or housing emergency.For Maine residents who received assistance, the campaign likely meant something very simple but important: a warm home during the coldest months of the year.You use AI every day. articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Supreme Court on Thursday said a bus conductor's right to access to justice is equal to that of a top bureaucrat, and granting out-of-turn
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Supreme Court on Thursday said a bus conductor's right to access to justice is equal to that of a top bureaucrat, and granting out-of-turn hearing to a litigant having the wherewithal to approach the SC would violate the right to speedy justice of millions languishing in the queue.A bench of Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana refused to entertain a plea for expeditious hearing of a petition by an additional district judge challenging his dismissal from service for corruption in 2022. His petition has been pending in Allahabad HC since 2022.Sacked for taking bribe, can’t allow early hearing: SC"When we grant early hearing to one litigant who has the resources to approach the SC, we do injustice to millions of litigants who are waiting for a hearing on their petitions," the bench said.In his plea for a direction to HC for expeditious disposal of his plea, the judge said he has suffered a lot in the last four years and that since his retirement is due on Nov 30, he would like to leave service with dignity.Referring to the pendency of more than 12 lakh cases in Allahabad HC, the bench told the counsel: "You are making a submission which is against the equal right to access to justice of every litigant, be it a bus conductor or a principal secretary. We will not request HC to grant out-of-turn hearing unless we are convinced about egregious circumstances in the case that warrant urgent hearing."The petitioner is one of the three additional district judges - Ashok Kumar Singh, Himanshu Bhatnagar and Rakesh Kumar Nain - who were dismissed from service on corruption charges through a full court resolution passed by Allahabad HC in May 2022.He complained that "no show-cause notice was ever issued to the petitioner and no opportunity was ever afforded to give any representation against the major penalty so imposed upon the petitioner, therefore, the resolution dated May 12, 2022, and the order dated May 17, 2022, by which the services of the petitioner were terminated, was passed in violation of principles of natural justice".The bench said that as the petitioner has been dismissed from service on charges of acceptance of bribe, it is not a fit case for requesting the HC to grant an out-of-turn hearing.The petitioner, who joined judicial service in Aug 1999 and was promoted as additional district judge in 2013, was accused of taking a Rs 6 lakh bribe to acquit a person in 2015. The inquiry and disciplinary proceedings were concluded in 2022, following which his services were terminated.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: A soldier gave these bean seeds to a family after serving in WWII; 80 years later, the same variety is entering Britain's heritage seed collection
articles.summary: A handful of bean seeds given to a family in France in 1946 has survived for decades through careful seed saving.
articles.body: A handful of bean seeds given to a family in France in 1946 has survived for decades through careful seed saving. According to Garden Organic, the dwarf French bean known as Weller's Blue was given to the father of the current donor by a soldier who had served in France during World War II. The donor has grown and saved the variety since 1970, and it was among 11 varieties added to the Heritage Seed Library's National Collection of Heritage Vegetables at the end of 2025. The addition was part of Sowing Your Seeds: Heritage Crops for a Resilient Future, a two-year project funded by the National Lottery Heritage Fund that is identifying and conserving heirloom and unusual vegetable varieties being grown across the Midlands.Weller's Blue bean and the Heritage Seed Library: how a WWII gift survived decadesThe Heritage Seed Library, run by Garden Organic, collects and conserves varieties in its National Collection of Heritage Vegetables. Through Sowing Your Seeds, the organisation has been searching across the Midlands for unusual and heirloom crops, along with the stories of the people and communities who have grown and saved them. The project began in 2025 as a two-year scheme supported by the National Lottery Heritage Fund.Before a variety is grown as part of the Heritage Seed Library's trials, Garden Organic researches its origins, including speaking with donors and searching historical seed catalogues. The organisation says it selects seeds that are not commercially available and have a proven record of performing well from seed to seed in the Midlands. This helps distinguish varieties that could add something valuable to the living collection from those already readily available through commercial seed suppliers. Weller's Blue was one of the varieties that made it through that process. Garden Organic describes it as a dwarf French bean and says its name comes from the donor's father, who received the seeds from a soldier who had served in France during WWII. The donor has subsequently grown and saved the bean since 1970.Sowing Your Seeds: how Garden Organic tests heritage vegetablesIn 2025, the first 19 varieties from the project were grown on site at Garden Organic's Heritage Seed Library. Ten were supplied by the UK Vegetable Gene Bank at Warwick University. Garden Organic says the Gene Bank holds 14,000 samples of vegetable crop seeds for plant breeders and researchers and is expected to contribute 20 varieties over the course of the project for potential addition to the Heritage Seed Library's living collection. The trials involved growing, measuring and monitoring the plants throughout the season. Garden Organic says the varieties were checked for germination, vigour and susceptibility to pests and disease, while the horticultural team recorded their characteristics to assess whether they were strong, successful, unique to the collection and consistent across the plants grown. Beans were hand-pollinated with tiny paintbrushes as part of the process.Of the original 19 varieties trialled in 2025, five were rejected because of poor germination, growth or variability. Two others, a beetroot and a carrot, are biennial crops and therefore needed another year of growth. Garden Organic lifted them at the end of the 2025 season and selected the strongest 40 to 50 plants for overwintering before replanting them for a second year. The remaining 11 varieties were successfully added to the Heritage Seed Library's permanent collection at the end of 2025. Garden Organic says the varieties are at risk of extinction and will be conserved and eventually shared with Heritage Seed Library members to grow.Grandfather's Bean, Golden Purslane and other varieties entering the collectionWeller's Blue was among a group of varieties with unusually long histories. Grandfather's Bean, a broad bean grown by the Burge family in Somerset, has been maintained by the same family for around 150 years. Garden Organic says the donor's father named it after his own great-grandfather, who was born in the 1830s. Another accession, Uncle Maurice's broad bean, has a history spanning 100 years, two continents, three cities and three gardens, according to Garden Organic. Borough Wonder lettuce can be traced to at least a 1945 Burgess Seeds Limited catalogue, while Golden Purslane was described by the English herbalist John Gerard in his 1597 work Generall Historie of Plantes.Other varieties accessioned in 2025 included Mega cress, the dwarf French bean Sigmacropper, Cheshunt Early Giant lettuce, Tip Top radish and the runner bean Portman. Garden Organic says Portman has been grown by the donor's family since the 1960s, with the current donor growing it since the 1970s.Bumpsteed Black gets another chance in 2026Not every unusual variety that entered the 2025 trials was immediately ready for the permanent collection. Runner bean Bumpsteed Black is one example. Garden Organic says the variety was originally a naturally occurring genetic variation, or “sport”, of a commercial bean that produced all-black seeds. Donor Roy Bumpsteed cultivated the characteristic for more than 20 years. Although the plants grew vigorously during the trial, some produced the traditional purple and black-speckled seeds as well as the all-black ones. Because the plants had cross-pollinated, the resulting seeds could not be kept reliably. Instead, Garden Organic's horticultural team traced the vines of the all-black plants back to their roots and protected the roots so the characteristic could be regrown the following year. Bumpsteed Black is therefore not one of the 11 varieties added to the collection at the end of 2025. Garden Organic says it is being given another chance and is due to be added in 2026 if the second trial successfully produces the desired all-black crop.Red orach, meanwhile, was successfully added to the permanent collection. Garden Organic says it is the first variety in the Heritage Seed Library collection known to produce two distinct types of seed on the same plant. The larger brown seeds have thinner coats, while the smaller black seeds have thicker coats. Their different dormancy levels stagger germination, which Garden Organic suggests could help the plant survive under different conditions. The work is continuing into 2026. Garden Organic says 27 new varieties are reaching the sowing phase this year, separate from the 19 varieties grown during the first round in 2025. The organisation is continuing to invite people in the Midlands to come forward with unusual or heritage vegetable varieties so that seeds maintained in gardens, allotments and families can be researched, trialled and potentially conserved for the future.You use AI every day.
