articles.title: Bill Nighy named best host at British Podcast Awards
articles.summary: The actor has become an agony uncle in what award organisers called an "irresistibly endearing series".
articles.body:
Actor Bill Nighy's reinvention as an agony uncle has earned him the award for best host at the British Podcast Awards, beating names such as Louis Theroux, Katherine Ryan and Lily Allen.

Nighy, 76, known for films including Love Actually, Living and the Underworld franchise, has now found success with what award organisers called his "irresistibly endearing series" Ill-Advised.

Billed as "a podcast for people who don't get out much and can't handle it when they do", the show sees Nighy dole out wry advice to listeners, and muse about life, music and books.

Other winners at the 10th annual British Podcast Awards on Thursday included Pete Wicks, Sophie and Jamie Laing, Peter Crouch and Alan Carr.

Pete Wicks' Man Made picked up two awards - best interview podcast and best health & wellbeing podcast.

Actor Sean Bean's birdwatching series Get Birding also won two prizes - best lifestyle podcast and best video innovation.

The Prison Radio Association's series about problem gambling, Hold or Fold, won the overall top prize for best podcast, and the award for best factual podcast.

Fans voted Hard Launch with Dan & Phil, hosted by the YouTube veterans, as the winner of the Listeners' Choice award.

articles.title: Russia’s Putin rules out ceasefire with Ukraine during speech in Moscow
articles.summary: Putin warned the West he would deploy nuclear weapons if necessary to defend the Russian Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad.
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin has ruled out a ceasefire on long-range strikes with Ukraine as Moscow steps up its campaign of aerial attacks on Kyiv .

“We are told: ‘Let them stop striking your refineries, and you will stop striking their ships.’ It is simply ridiculous,” Putin said on Thursday at the Valdai political forum in Moscow.

The remarks followed a meeting between United States President Donald Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in New York on September 22, when Zelenskyy said Kyiv was ready to cease strikes on Russian oil refineries and other energy facilities if Moscow also stopped its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.

Speaking at the forum of the Moscow-based think tank, Putin said Ukraine had “partially achieved its objectives” with ⁠these strikes, with attacks on Russian ⁠oil refineries having cost the country 1 percent of its gross domestic product (GDP), but added that Russia ⁠was now responding in kind.

Russia has ramped up long-range strikes, targeting Ukraine’s steel companies as well as supply chains, notably in the rail sector. Ukraine accuses Moscow of deliberately hitting civilian targets and keeping Kyiv on a near-constant state of alert as it braces for another tough winter.

A Russian drone struck a school in Kyiv on Thursday, according to city officials, as the Ukrainian capital endured relentless aerial attacks. No casualties were reported as children and staff at the school were in shelters when the drone hit.

Putin added that Russia would prefer to end the conflict in Ukraine through talks and wanted it to ⁠be a neutral ⁠country after the end ⁠of hostilities.

He warned the West not to escalate the standoff over Ukraine by threatening the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, which is wedged between Poland and Lithuania, and pledged to defend it with nuclear weapons if necessary.

“If it comes to a direct attack on the Russian Federation – in this case, we are referring to Kaliningrad, and perhaps other territories as well – the question of the Russian Federation deploying all the weapons at our country’s disposal will, of course, inevitably and immediately be on the agenda,” he said.

Putin’s comments followed a diplomatic note which NATO said this week it had received from Russia, warning the Western military alliance it would be ready to resort to nuclear weapons if NATO attempted to cut off Russia’s Baltic exclave.

Putin warned that cycles of escalation in international conflict ⁠could quickly lead to dangerous scenarios. “We must realise that the moment when nothing can be changed any longer may come very quickly and unexpectedly for everyone. The logic of escalating, increasingly harsh retaliatory measures leads to a fatal point of no return,” ⁠he said.

On the contrary, in the event of a “favourable scenario”, Putin said the assets of Western companies that Moscow had seized could potentially be returned. Putin last month ordered the seizure of businesses and assets of Swiss food giant Nestle, French retailer Auchan, the former Leroy Merlin DIY chain and German wholesaler and food retailer Metro.

articles.title: Of 97 left out in Goa, 88 are back, 3 others are Portuguese citizens: EC
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The office of the Goa chief electoral officer on Thursday said 88 of the 97 voters in the state whose names could not be included in the roll
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The office of the Goa chief electoral officer on Thursday said 88 of the 97 voters in the state whose names could not be included in the roll due to an alleged ECINet issue have been added back after their duly filled Form 6 was accepted. However, he also revealed that three of these 97 electors are Portuguese passport holders while six others were electors currently based outside India."In respect of voters who are currently residing outside India, officials are making efforts to establish and maintain contact with them for necessary action," the CEO said while sharing the status report on the 97 cases on X.Section 9 of the Constitution disallows dual citizenship. Goans born before 1961 in former Portuguese territories, as well as their kids and grandchildren, can apply for a Portuguese passport based on a citizen card issued by the Portuguese authorities after verifying their birth/descent documents. Portugal recognises dual citizenship; however, since dual citizenship is not allowed in India, anybody who acquires a foreign passport must surrender his Indian passport. As per Sec 9 of the Citizenship Act, 1955, a person's Indian citizenship automatically ceases upon acquiring foreign citizenship.Thus, three of the Portuguese passport holders in Goa may be classified as non-citizens, making them ineligible to be enrolled as Indian electors, said a source.Incidentally, Portuguese passport holders form 3% of the cohort of 97 electors for which the Goa CEO had repeatedly written to the EC after the ERO could not add them back via ERONet, leading the ECs to also raise questions on why access for such changes was 'centralised' and not available to the field officers. The issue was further amplified by the opposition parties after The Indian Express reported on the alleged internal notes of the election commissioners in this regard.EC sources on Thursday said the due diligence by the ERO the second time around may have served the purpose of SIR, as it is aimed at eliminating ineligible persons from the voters' list. Also, the fact that the issue was detected at the ERO level proves that the absolute right to add or delete a voter, based on verification, remains with the field officers, an EC officer told TOI.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Putin says Russia will use ‘all weapons’ in its arsenal if any of its territory is attacked
articles.summary: President Vladimir Putin on Thursday reiterated Moscow’s long-held position that Russia is not planning to attack European countries but will respond to aggression with “all weapons” in its arsenal.
articles.body: President Vladimir Putin on Thursday reiterated Moscow’s long-held position that Russia is not planning to attack European countries but will respond to aggression with “all weapons” in its arsenal. In remarks at a foreign policy forum, Putin accused the West and Europe of escalating tensions by talking about preparing for a war with Moscow in the coming years, conducting military drills in the Baltic Sea, and seizing Russian vessels. His remarks followed Moscow’s warning to NATO that it would not hesitate to use nuclear weapons to defend Kaliningrad should any members of the military alliance try to cut off the Baltic exclave from the rest of Russia. Several Russian embassies in Europe this week issued statements that said Moscow has “information that NATO is preparing (an) air and naval blockade of Kaliningrad and (the) Kaliningrad region.” They accused European leaders of “playing a dangerous game” by saying Russia might attack another country or ramp up a campaign of destabilizing attacks with drones and sabotage. Moscow has called the allegations absurd. “There should be no mistake — Russia would be ready to use all its arsenal, including nuclear weapons, to defend its territory if NATO countries try to isolate (the) Kaliningrad region from the rest of the country,” the Russian Embassy in Ireland said in its statement on Tuesday. Asked at the Valdai Club forum Thursday whether Russia was on the cusp of a war with NATO or whether both were trying to intimidate each other, Putin said: “It’s not intimidation, it’s a response to an attempt to intimidate us.” Putin said that “everything is written correctly” in the earlier warning to NATO. “If it comes to a direct attack on the Russian Federation — in this case we mean Kaliningrad, or maybe some other territories — of course, inevitably and immediately the question of Russian Federation using all weapons at the disposal of our country will appear on the agenda,” he said. Putin didn’t specify whether Moscow would use nuclear weapons but said it has arms that “no one else has” and would determine which to use in case of an attack. NATO pushed back against Russian nuclear rhetoric NATO spokesperson Allison Hart confirmed Wednesday that Russia had sent a written message to the U.S.-led military alliance. “We strongly denounce the threat of force, including any irresponsible nuclear rhetoric,” she said in a statement. Hart insisted NATO is not targeting Kaliningrad and had sent a reply noting that “NATO is a defensive alliance and none of our activities or exercises pose a risk to any part of Russia.” NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said Wednesday the bloc’s response to the message was “short and concise.” “Basically what we said is, ‘Hey, listen, we are defensive alliance, and stop the nuclear threat. This is absolutely not called for and not helpful,’” Rutte told Euronews. NATO’s response also urged Russia to stop its “unprovoked war of aggression against Ukraine,” now in its fifth year. The Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad sits between NATO members Poland and Lithuania. It is home to Russia’s main Baltic navy base and other military assets, and nuclear-capable Iskander missiles are deployed there. Western military officers have said that key military installations in Kaliningrad would be a likely first target should Russia ever attack any NATO ally. NATO allies have conducted military exercises in the Baltic Sea region in recent months. More are planned in October. It launched Operation Baltic Sentry there last year to protect communication cables and pipelines. On Aug. 18, NATO held an exercise over northern Poland and the Baltic region involving several aircraft, including an EA-37B Compass Call — a sophisticated American plane that can jam communications and radar, the U.S. Air Forces in Europe said. Defense analysts believe the unannounced, large-scale exercise would not have been welcomed by the Kremlin. Rutte urges continued focus on supporting Ukraine European leaders and intelligence services have warned that Russia could be ready to strike at another country within a few years, especially if it wins its war on Ukraine. Rutte told Euronews that Russia is trying “to divide us and lose the focus” on defending Ukraine. “We will not,” he said, adding that the best way to respond is to provide Kyiv with more support. “That’s the message. Calm, carry on, keep the support for Ukraine going. That’s how we deal with it,” Rutte said.

articles.title: Larry Fitzgerald Q&A: NFL icon talks breast cancer awareness for his late mother, friendship with John McCain
articles.summary: Larry Fitzgerald revealed how losing his mother to breast cancer in 2003 inspired the DraftKings Pink 'Em campaign, which has raised over $700,000.
articles.body: Former Arizona Cardinals star Larry Fitzgerald has turned the personal pain of losing his mother to breast cancer into a mission to help families confronting the disease. Fitzgerald’s mother, Carol, died from breast cancer in 2003. His foundation has since partnered with DraftKings on its annual Pink ’Em campaign, which has raised more than $700,000 for breast cancer awareness, research and patient support since launching in 2019. Fitzgerald spoke with OutKick about the campaign, the influence of his mother, his friendship with the late Sen. John McCain, the relationships that defined his 17 seasons with the Cardinals and the current NFL season. Questions and answers have been shortened for brevity and focus. Q: Your foundation’s partnership with DraftKings through the Pink ’Em campaign has raised more than $700,000 for breast cancer awareness. What does that mean to you personally? Larry Fitzgerald: Well, it means a lot that you can raise this type of awareness together in a partnership. And I think that’s what makes partnerships so special, especially when you have one as longstanding as this. Every single year, obviously, we’re raising money for a wonderful cause, but also getting people on our platform to play in our Pink ’Em campaign. And it’s a win-win for everybody. We get to raise awareness, and it’s a beautiful thing. Q: When did you first become passionate about this cause? Fitzgerald: In 2003, I lost my mother to breast cancer. And so this has been something that’s near and dear to my heart. I have a couple other family members who’ve battled it. People in my organization at our foundation have done it as well. And so it’s something that I live with, I think about, I hear about often in terms of treatments and cutting-edge results that are happening from some of the life sciences that are occurring now. And so this is something, I live this every single day. Q: When you think back on your mother, what do you think she would think of where your career has gone and how you’ve created this foundation and championed this cause? Fitzgerald: My mom was in the nonprofit space. So I know that it would be something that she would be happy about. As a child, I was always going to events that she was either a part of, or she was a part of organizations that supported them. So it was always a part of the fabric of who we were as a family. My hope is that she would be proud of the work that we’re continuing to do. And I think she would want me to continue to stay motivated, to not take my foot off the gas and keep my focus on serving. Q: What’s the biggest thing your mother taught you while you were growing up that you’ve carried throughout your life? Fitzgerald: Well, just to be thoughtful and compassionate. There’s a lot of people out there that are in need. And sometimes somebody needs just a helping hand, a hello, a thank you, "How are you doing?" Just to be seen and thought about. Those things are really important. They were important to her. And I always saw that she would always do that. And it’s something that I tried to implement when I was a youngster and still to this day. SAM ACHO Q&A: FORMER NFL PLAYER AND ESPN ANALYST SPEAKS OUT ON CIVILITY AND ACCOUNTABILITY IN SPORTS AND MEDIA Q: How do you think that helped shape you during your football career? Fitzgerald: It’s something that I think is a part of you no matter what you do. It doesn’t matter if it’s in my current occupation or my former occupation. Being thoughtful, caring, really enjoying cultivating relationships and developing relationships is something that is important in anything that you do in life. It doesn’t matter if you’re on TV, if you’re a garbage man, if you’re a doctor. Having that human connectivity is important. Q: One of the friendships you made during your career that really stood out was with the late John McCain. Fitzgerald: Yeah, I mean, Senator McCain was a wonderful man and influence in my life. He’s one of the people that I credit with helping me mature and seeing the world in a different light. Traveling to Vietnam and doing a lot of his events with him opened my eyes and my world up to things I never would have thought I’d been exposed to. And so, really, really thankful and appreciative of the relationship that I’ve had with him and so many others. It doesn’t have to be one of the greatest U.S. senators and patriots that we’ve had in our country. It could be anybody that you meet in an elevator. That’s what I really enjoy about fostering relationships. Q: How did he help you change your worldview? Fitzgerald: Well, I mean, he just opened his world to me, showed me different things, gave me tours of the Senate, let me sit in hearings and confirmation hearings and things that I would have never experienced without him allowing me to be a part of it. And so I think that’s huge. It says a lot about who he is to take somebody in that didn’t necessarily have a view into that type of life. Q: Did you agree with Senator McCain politically? Fitzgerald: I don’t know if I would say I agree with everything Senator McCain — I don’t know if I agree with everything that any senator or politician believes in. I kind of have my own political views that I keep to myself. But I can attest to the quality of man that he was and the contributions that he made to our country. Q: What does it say about the connection you had that, even if you disagreed on some political views, you were still open to letting him help shape your worldview? Fitzgerald: Well, I think that’s something I talked about when he gave me one of the best honors of my life, to be able to speak at his funeral, is that he embraced the differences. And it would be really nice to be able to see that thoughtfulness in the way that our country is governed like it was when he was around. And so I’m very thankful that he poured into me and poured into so many of his other constituents. Q: Nowadays, there are a lot of people who don’t agree politically, including athletes and politicians. What do you think people could learn from your friendship with John McCain? Fitzgerald: I don’t know if I would say I did not agree with him politically. I did say I didn’t agree with everything politically. I really enjoyed my relationship with him. It would be nice to be able to see people have civil discourse without heartburn or hard feelings for somebody who doesn’t necessarily see eye to eye with them on something. So I think that’s something that we can all learn. I still look back at when he was running for president and somebody at one of his political rallies said something that wasn’t true about President Obama. And then he quickly debunked it. And that was a very powerful message, like, "Hey, he’s an opponent, an opponent that I really want to beat, but I’m not going to allow you to say things that are not true." And I think that was something that I really admired about him. Q: Do you see yourself cultivating any friendships with politicians nowadays? Fitzgerald: Yeah, I’m friendly with a lot of people. Friendly with people that are politicians. I’m friendly with people that are doctors. I’m friendly with people that are lawyers. I’m friendly with most people. Q: Another thing about you that fascinated a lot of people throughout your career is how loyal you stayed to the Arizona Cardinals. Looking back on it, what grounded you there and kept you in Arizona? Fitzgerald: Well, I’ve always been one of those people who likes to finish what they started. They brought me there to do a job, and I wanted to make sure I did the job that I was brought there to do. And a lot of times there’s other opportunities that might be more attractive, but I really like to kind of do the things that I want to do in the places that I’m at. And the grass is not always greener on the other side. Q: Were you ever tempted to consider an offer from another team? Fitzgerald: Not seriously. No, not seriously. No. Q: What was your best moment with the Cardinals? Fitzgerald: I mean, to take one moment from 17 years, I would say probably playing in a Super Bowl. But that’s not what I think about the most. I look back in those times, I think about the relationships with the coaches, support staff, my teammates, management, ownership. Those are the things that I think I take the most joy from. It’s just the wonderful people I was able to work with. Q: Who are some of the people specifically from the Cardinals whom you remember most fondly? Fitzgerald: Mark Dalton, Lisa Manning, Steve Ryan. Obviously, Michael Bidwill was — he gave me my job, he drafted me. Rod Graves, Dennis Green, Bruce Arians, Ken Whisenhunt and so many teammates as well. I mean, I could be here all day naming people who influenced my life in a positive way. Q: Bruce Arians is famous for having a personality that is a little different from other coaches, at least in terms of what fans and the media could see. In your experience, was he unique compared to the other coaches you played for? Fitzgerald: I wouldn’t say he was too much different than any other coaches. He never bit his tongue. He told you what he thought. I think that was really cool, to be able to have somebody that was so transparent. You never had to worry about or wonder what he was thinking. And that made it a lot easier to play for him. When you know exactly what the expectations are going to be every day. But all the coaches are different, and they’re effective in their own right. Q: What was your favorite memory with Coach Arians that people may not know about? Fitzgerald: I would say just seeing his heart. Him and his wife, Chris, were really big on adoption and foster parents. And I had no idea how many thousands of kids are in the foster care system in Arizona. And the work that he would do through his foundation would do a really good job of pairing foster parents with foster children, trying to give stability to so many of our young people that are in need. And so, seeing that human, compassionate side of him was something that really resonated with me. Q: Do you think he could make a coaching comeback today? Fitzgerald: I think so. If that was something he wanted to do and his wife allowed him to do it, I think he would be really good. I mean, he’s one of the best play-callers I’ve ever been around. He has a way to really connect with his players. And also, I think he really does a good job with quarterbacks. You look at what he did with Ben Roethlisberger, what he did with Andrew Luck, what he did with Carson Palmer and everywhere that he’s gone. Tom Brady won a championship down there in Tampa. He’s done a hell of a job every single stop he’s made. Q: The Cardinals have a big game this week against the Giants. Both teams are dealing with veteran backups. As someone who has played with a lot of veteran quarterbacks, sometimes backup quarterbacks, what do you expect from this game and the two teams moving forward as they navigate their quarterback situations? Fitzgerald: Yeah, the Giants have unfortunately got kind of bit with a rash of injuries. They lost Brian Burns, their best edge rusher, and then losing Jaxson Dart to a season injury. It’s a tough thing to deal with, but injuries are part of the game. I think the Cardinals are a much healthier, fresher team. They played their last two opponents in the Seahawks and the 49ers, who I think are both playoff teams, really, really hard. And so, I like their chances to be able to get a win this week in the Meadowlands. Q: Do you stay in touch with any of the players and coaches currently on the Cardinals? Do you ever give them advice or coaching? Fitzgerald: No, not advice. I’m not one to give unsolicited advice, but still have great relationships with a few of the players. I played with guys like Budda Baker, and so I have a really good relationship with guys on the squad still. Q: Who are your top five wide receivers in the NFL this year? Fitzgerald: It’s hard. I haven’t had a chance to watch every single team play. But they got some terrific play in the game right now. And even guys who you thought their skill set started to diminish, you watch guys like Davante Adams still had an amazing game last week against the Broncos, eight catches, 140 yards receiving. So, I mean, any given week, somebody can rise to the occasion and be special. Q: What about quarterbacks? Fitzgerald: Again, that’s tough, man. Obviously, Josh Allen’s coming off an MVP season and Patrick Mahomes coming off a knee injury and still looking just as good as he’s ever looked. And the throw that Lamar Jackson made last week to put his team in position against the Cowboys to get that game-winning field goal was great. You got to throw — let me think who else you put in that conversation. Joe Burrow’s looked really good statistically. He’s been throwing around and making a lot of plays. Bo Nix is playing good ball. So, I mean, there’s a lot of good players out there. Q: Giants quarterback Jaxson Dart looked very good in Week 1 before going down. What should fans expect from him when he returns from injury? Fitzgerald: Yeah, I mean, he’s really showed a lot of promise. I really like the way he leads. I enjoyed watching him at Ole Miss when he was down there. And then every single year, it looks like he’s just taking more steps in the right direction. So it sucks to see him go down the way he did and affect his team the way that that’s going to affect him. But I think he’s got a really, really bright future. And I think anybody who’s a Giants fan or football fan in general should be excited about it. Q: As a star wide receiver who played with many different quarterbacks, what kind of impact will Malik Nabers have to make for the Giants to have a good season? Fitzgerald: Well, Malik is coming off an injury himself, and so it’s really cool to be able to see him take that ownership and leadership position. He’s the best player on that offense now, and I think he can still go out there and win regardless. Jameis Winston is a veteran guy. He’s been in the league a really long time. And so, will there be a drop-off? Possibly. But I don’t think it will be one that would hurt him in a negative way. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! Q: Jaxson Dart introduced President Donald Trump during the offseason, which received a range of reactions. As someone who had a friendship with a politician, what was your reaction when you saw that? Fitzgerald: Yeah, I don’t know what his relationship was or is with President Trump. And I don’t know how that came about. But he made a decision that he felt was best for himself. And that’s what we all do as human beings. We make decisions based on the information that we have. And he did that. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Q: Would you ever consider introducing a president or a politician running for office? articles.title: TikTok and Instagram posts 'don't warn hikers about dangers'
articles.summary: Rescues of 18 to 24-year-olds more than double in Wales and England since 2019, rescuers say.
articles.body:
Social media posts on TikTok and Instagram show the beauty of wild places without warning about the danger walkers can face, mountain rescuers have said.

"Too many people influenced by these posts are ending up in the mountains unprepared," said Nick Phillips from Mountain Rescue England and Wales (MREW).

It recorded emergencies involving 18 to 24-year-olds almost doubled from 2019-2024, with the four largest teams in Wales all on track for record high call outs in 2026.

A team responsible for Wales' tallest mountain said the pressure on volunteers was "unsustainable", a concern echoed by the team near Brecon that said demand "keeps rising".

Llanberis Mountain Rescue Team (LMRT) is Wales' busiest and had its most calls in a month in August - 59, or two a day - and it was not just the prolonged warm weather.

The team has recorded a steady rise in rescue operations every year going back to 2020, when it had 147 call outs all year.

It has called for a "serious conversation " as it is set to hit 450 rescues by the end of the year, having already attended 359.

MREW said 18 to 24-year-olds became the biggest age group in need of rescuing in 2024 when they were involved in 314 incidents, up 89% from 166 in 2019.

It added: "We are not criticising people who want to go into the mountain based on what they have seen in a post... but we need to be balanced with the reality."

"This year's increase has been really worrying", said LMRT volunteer Tom Carrick.

Speaking to Newyddion S4C, he added that if the rise continues at a similar pace, the service would not be able to cope.

"We've had 30 new volunteers joining the team. We're in September now and already we're seeing a lot of burnout among volunteers, some who've been here for years and others newer.

LMRT said the main concern was the number of people turning up to climb mountains without experience and suitable kit.

"A photograph or video of Crib Goch can make an exposed grade one scramble look like just another route to the summit.

"What it doesn't show is how intimidating that ridge can be in cloud, rain or strong winds or how quickly a manageable situation can become a serious emergency."

Increased demand is being reported by most teams in Wales.

Brecon Mountain Rescue Team, which had 70 call outs in 2020, has already had 80.

Ogwen Mountain Rescue Team, which also works in Eryri National Park, or Snowdonia, said it had 107 call outs in 2020 but is projected to get more than 200 this year.

Central and Brecon Mountain Rescue (CBMRT) had 89 calls in 2020 and could hit 200 this year.

"Reaching 150 call outs already this year, after our busiest ever year last year, brings home the scale of the commitment," said Huw Jones, who has been with CBMRT for 45 years.

"My concern is how we sustain that commitment if demand keeps rising. Volunteers' time and energy are finite.

"We cannot assume that more and more can be absorbed indefinitely, and we need to talk about that now so teams can continue to be there for people in the years ahead."

MREW said Instagram, TikTok and X were putting beauty spots around the world in the spotlight, including peaks in Wales such as Yr Wyddfa and Pen y Fan.

"Wonderful places to go, but what the posts don't capture how you get there," Phillips said.

It is leading what he hopes will be a "culture change", engaging ambassadors including TV explorer Ben Fogle and reaching out to social media influencers.

"We want to capture people at home to hopefully reduce these avoidable call outs," it said.

"People need to be aware they are in a dangerous place."

In 1995, Caradoc Jones who lives in Helsby, Cheshire, became the first Welshman to reach the summit of Everest and has climbed in some of the world's most dangerous and remote landscapes.

He welcomed the fact more people are exploring mountains but agrees a culture shift is needed and wants more to be done on social media to warn people about the realities of mountaineering.

Jones also suggested mountain rescue teams should be funded by the government instead of donations.

The Welsh government said: "Our mountain rescue teams do a fantastic job supporting people across Wales, often in challenging and demanding circumstances, and we thank them for their dedication and hard work.

"We recognise in our programme of government the important role that the voluntary sector plays in delivering public services and are engaging with mountain rescue teams to discuss support."

articles.title: Supreme Court stays hanging of 2008 Gujarat serial blasts convict
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Thursday stayed the execution of the death penalty of Ahmed Bawa alias Abbu Abubakar Barelvi, who was an operative of the
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Thursday stayed the execution of the death penalty of Ahmed Bawa alias Abbu Abubakar Barelvi, who was an operative of the terror outfit Indian Mujahideen (IM) and was convicted for the 2008 Ahmedabad serial bomb blasts that left 56 people dead. A bench of Justices Vikram Nath, A G Masih and Sandeep Mehta issued notice to the Gujarat government on Bawa's plea against the Gujarat high court verdict, which upheld his death sentence awarded by the trial court.The HC on July 7 upheld the death sentences of 38 operatives of IM in the 2008 blasts case, citing the large number of casualties. It also upheld life imprisonment given to 11 other convicts, holding that their roles in terror training camps in Gujarat and Kerala and logistical support to the conspiracy had been proved. On July 26, 2008, a series of 21 bomb blasts ripped through different areas of Ahmedabad, killing 56 people and leaving over 200 injured. The HC had rejected all appeals filed by the convicts and confirmed the Feb 2022 judgment of the special court, which had sentenced 38 IM members to death and 11 others to life imprisonment. articles.title: Government backs SCO connectivity, but PM's Pakistan visit uncertain
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: India's participation in the SCO meeting of national coordinators in Islamabad to firm up the calendar for high-level meetings has sparked
articles.body: NEW DELHI: India's participation in the SCO meeting of national coordinators in Islamabad to firm up the calendar for high-level meetings has sparked speculation about whether PM Modi would travel to Pakistan for the heads of state summit next year. Modi has missed only one of the seven in-person summits since India became a full member of the Eurasian bloc in 2017, but officials said his past attendance is no guarantee of a visit even for a multilateral event to Pakistan, a country India has come to describe as a serial practitioner of terrorism.Additional secretary Alok Dimri travelled to Pakistan this week for the national coordinators' meeting, as first reported by TOI on Monday. The first such visit from India to Pakistan since the 2025 Pahalgam terrorist attack highlighted how SCO, which is dominated by China and Russia, has remained insulated from India-Pakistan tensions, unlike the more modest Saarc regional framework.For a PM visit, though, as official sources said, India will factor in Pakistan's continued support for cross-border terrorism before making a final decision. The same is likely to apply for the meetings of defence and foreign ministers heading into the main summit, as India seeks tangible and irreversible action by Pakistan against cross-border terrorism to make the overall environment conducive for any substantive engagement.After the meeting this week, Pakistan PM Shehbaz Sharif will soon write to leaders of all member states inviting them for the SCO heads of state summit. He had last invited Modi for the heads of govt meeting in Islamabad in 2024, but India had then sent external affairs minister S Jaishankar, who usually represents India in that meeting.Modi attends the meetings of the Council of Heads of State (CHS), the supreme decision-making body of SCO, which meets annually on a rotational basis in the country chairing SCO. Pakistan assumed chairmanship from Kyrgyzstan at the Bishkek summit last month.Although Modi did skip the Kazakhstan summit in 2024, India will likely weigh multiple geopolitical factors before deciding on his potential visit to Pakistan, apart from Pakistan-backed terrorism. India's engagement with SCO facilitates the ongoing normalisation of relations with China while preserving its strategic and longstanding ties with Russia. Ironically, counterterrorism and security cooperation is one key reason for Delhi's engagements with the grouping that also helps India with Central Asian connectivity and regional security in Afghanistan, while reinforcing strategic autonomy.Dimri was greeted warmly in Pakistan, with an official photo showing him standing next to Pakistan deputy PM and foreign minister Ishaq Dar. Dimri said the national coordinators had finalised an agenda for common wellbeing and prosperity with focus on connectivity, trade and transit. "This programme will continue for a year and will culminate with the Islamabad Summit."Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Putin warns West that Russia is prepared to use ‘all weapons’ to protect Kaliningrad
articles.summary: Russian President Vladimir Putin has warned the West against escalating the war in Ukraine, saying Moscow is prepared to use “all weapons” in its arsenal — including nuclear — if its Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad comes under attack.
articles.body: Russian President Vladimir Putin has warned the West against escalating the war in Ukraine, saying Moscow is prepared to use “all weapons” in its arsenal — including nuclear — if its Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad comes under attack. Speaking at the Valdai Discussion Club in Moscow on Thursday, the Russian leader said he had no plans to attack any European country but was prepared to respond to Western aggression if necessary and referenced the Russian territory sandwiched between NATO members Poland and Lithuania. His warning follows recent military drills by NATO near Kaliningrad that the bloc has described as defensive exercises to strengthen deterrence. Those exercises have prompted strong concerns from Moscow, which warned in late September it would retaliate if NATO attempted to blockade the exclave by air or sea. “The drills in the Baltic Sea, following one another … Then the attempts to arrest our ships and vessels. All this is an escalation. And then we began to hear statements regarding the Kaliningrad region,” Putin said. “If it comes to direct attack against the Russian Federation, in this case on Kaliningrad and possibly some other territories, of course the issue of using all weapons in our country’s arsenal will inevitably and unavoidably emerge on the agenda. This is unavoidable,” he cautioned. NATO, several European countries and the United Kingdom have accused Russia of conducting hybrid warfare against them, including cyberattacks, sabotage and espionage attempts, aimed at breaking their support for Ukraine. Russia’s war in Ukraine, dubbed by Moscow as a “special military operation,” is now in its fifth year, but Putin shows no sign of slowing his offensive and has instead intensified strikes on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure and its capital city of Kyiv ahead of an anticipated bitterly cold winter. But recent Ukrainian drone strikes on Russia’s oil refineries have led to widespread fuel shortages, shattering the illusion that the consequences of the conflict are far removed from ordinary Russians. Long queues of cars at fuel stations have been seen in major cities, while hits on Russia’s largest online retailers have increased pressure on the already strained wartime economy. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky regularly refers to Ukrainian drone strikes deep inside Russian territory as “long-range sanctions,” designed to reduce Russia’s revenues, military capacity and push the Kremlin into negotiations. In his speech Thursday to foreign policy and international affairs academics, Putin admitted the Ukrainian strikes were taking a toll on Russia’s economy, saying they had cost Russia 1% of its gross domestic product (GDP) and that Ukrainian military maneuvers in the Black Sea have taken out over 100 Russian ships. However, Putin also made clear he remains undeterred. “In the Black Sea — that’s a combat zone; we struck military vessels and ships transporting military cargo, and we hardly ever made a mistake. Throughout this whole saga, they [Ukraine] have knocked out over 100 of our ships. Well, we started hitting back, and now we’re being bombarded from every direction with appeals: “Oh, please stop doing that,” Putin said. “It’s the same story with our oil refineries; they (Ukraine) openly declared their goal was to damage our economy. Did they succeed? Partially — by our estimates, we lost about one percent of our GDP. And it was done deliberately — these are civilian targets, after all. Well, they got a mirror-image response,” Putin added, sidestepping that it was Moscow who launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Putin’s admission of the economic toll comes just one day after he told newly elected members of the State Duma — the lower house of Russia’s parliament, which predictably saw the United Russia party that backs Putin hold onto its majority — that the Russian economy was stable. Taking the opportunity to swipe at Ukraine, the Russian president on Wednesday derided Kyiv’s reliance on financial assistance from its Western allies. “Mistakes, especially now, are absolutely unacceptable,” he warned parliamentarians. “Unlike some, and we won’t point fingers, Russia can’t run around the world humiliating (itself) by begging for handouts with an outstretched hand,” he said. “Firstly, because, as I have already said, it is humiliating. Secondly, no one is going to give us anything, and we know that very well. And thirdly, and most importantly, we do not need it. Russia’s financial system and economy are secure,” he continued. While signaling in recent weeks that he does not intend to draw back from the war in Ukraine, Putin also said he would prefer the conflict to end through talks. Ahead of the election, Putin had said the results would show Russians are united by the military and its goals — though the Levada Center, an independent pollster, found in an August poll that 59% of Russians favored moving to peace talks. In a further sign that Putin does not plan to slow down the “special military operation,” budget documents reviewed by Reuters show that Russia plans to spend 17.1 trillion rubles ($205.112 billion) on defense in 2027, about 27% more than originally budgeted and the highest level since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

articles.title: Cornell survey showed increase in reports of nonconsensual sexual contact among female undergrads
articles.summary: The findings are receiving renewed attention after the local districts attorney said it was reopening a criminal investigation into an alleged 2024 gang rape at the university.
articles.body: More than 35% of female undergraduates surveyed at Cornell University reported experiencing nonconsensual sexual contact involving physical force, threats of force or incapacitation, according to a poll conducted last year, a figure that was up from 23% in 2023. Overall, the survey found that 15% of all of the respondents reported such experiences compared to about 11% in 2021 and 2023 surveys. Cornell notes in its survey that a total of 6,000 students received email invitations to participate and only 926 responded, resulting in a 15% response rate, with 519 of those responding identifying as women. According to the report, the 2025 response rate was lower than in previous years. The findings are receiving renewed attention after the Tompkins County District Attorney’s Office said it was reopening a criminal investigation into an alleged 2024 gang rape at Cornell’s fraternity house. Eight universities that surveyed their students on nonconsensual sexual contact using the Higher Education Sexual Misconduct and Awareness Survey in 2024 showed rates lower than 30%. In that survey, Washington University in St. Louis reported a result of 26.9% of respondents saying they had experienced nonconsensual sexual contact involving physical force or the inability to consent or stop the actions. Georgetown University reported 25.3% on the same issue in the same survey. Yale University and the University of Pennsylvania, which reported rates of 14.4% and 16.7%, also account for nonconsensual “penetration or sexual touching.” Under state law, Cornell is required to conduct a campus sexual violence survey every two years. In 2017, the school developed the Survey of Sexual Assault and Related Misconduct and has administered it every two years since 2019. In Cornell’s survey, alcohol was involved in many of the reported incidents, while the use of other recreational drugs was less common. Among the undergraduate female respondents, most reported that the incidents took place inside residence halls, fraternity chapter houses or annexes and off-campus houses. Studies have shown that incidents of sexual violence frequently occur on college campuses during the first two months of the school year, a period referred to as the “red zone,” when students are going to parties and other events. According to the American Psychological Association, which cites a 2008 study, researchers have found that 50% of campus sexual assaults occur during the red zone and affect new students. In a civil lawsuit filed earlier this month, an unidentified woman alleged that on Oct. 19, 2024, members of the Chi Phi fraternity sexually assaulted her for hours and she was pressured to take ketamine. The woman also said that one member had sent a message encouraging others to take part in the attack. The fraternity chapter was barred from campus following the alleged assault, but no one was criminally charged. “While we cannot discuss the specific allegations during pending litigation, we take this matter seriously,” Chi Phi National fraternity said in a statement Sept. 18. “Our responsibility is to approach this with care for those affected and respect for a fair legal process.” Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten said the woman’s lawsuit prompted him to reopen the criminal case. The case will be presented to a grand jury to determine if criminal indictments should be issued against the seven fraternity members named in the suit. The suit said that some of the fraternity members involved were able to “mitigate their conduct” by writing essays to the university. In a previous statement, Cornell said it launched a Title IX investigation that resulted in “a range of sanctions, which included expulsions and suspensions from Cornell. None of the individuals charged were offered the opportunity to write essays as a sole consequence of their involvement.” “Any suggestion that the university did not impose consequential punishments for those involved is false,” the statement said. The lawsuit has sparked intense outrage over the handling of the initial sexual assault case in 2024. Van Houten defended his office’s decision not to seek criminal charges at the time, saying that the woman did not allege that she was raped or drugged against her will. According to Van Houten, the woman had described in a statement “her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious, and consensual.” The woman’s attorney, Thomas P. Giuffra, has said that she was “traumatized” and “numb” in the days after the assault and was “unable to function or accept the horror of what happened.” In a written statement, the woman said she wants “to recover from this trauma but it is extremely difficult.” “It affects every aspect of my life,” she said in the statement. “It will haunt me and be part of me the rest of my life.” The attorney for one of the men accused in the lawsuit of sexual assault, Scott Kretzschmar, denied he harmed the woman in any way, saying the lawsuit was “not only intentionally dishonest but morally repugnant.” “He’s done nothing wrong other than being irresponsible and immature and inappropriate and ugly in those Snapchats,” the attorney, Jeremy Saland, said Wednesday. “But in terms of a crime, he was not involved in a crime, and nor was he aware of one because if he was, he would have reported.” Another one of the fraternity brothers, Gillio Lopes, who is being accused in the lawsuit of sexual assault, also denied this allegation. “The public narrative now being advanced is incomplete and, in important respects, inconsistent with the record developed during the Cornell process, including many of Jane Doe’s own statements,” his attorney Andrew Miltenberg said. Miltenberg said that during the initial investigation dozens of people were interviewed, there were multiple days of hearings and testimony, and an investigative report. “It is these statements, contemporaneous communications, and other evidence that provide important context that is absent from the current public account. Those differences, and the evidence bearing on them, will severely compromise Jane Doe’s narrative,” he said in a statement. The attorney for one of the other men did not respond to a request for comment. It’s not clear if the others have obtained counsel. If you or someone you know has been sexually assaulted, call the National Sexual Assault Hotline at 1-800-656-4673. The hotline, run by the Rape, Abuse, & Incest National Network (RAINN), can put you in contact with your local rape crisis center. You can also access RAINN’s online chat service at rainn.org/get-help.

articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Thursday rejected a petition by Mamata Banerjee-headed TMC faction seeking de-freezing of its three bank accounts on grounds that the party required funds to carry out political activities, such as holding rallies and meetings.Challenging Calcutta HC's order allowing only meeting of day-to-day expenses of the party from these accounts, senior advocate A M Singhvi said the party's three Indian Bank accounts, which have been given a clean chit by the Enforcement Directorate (ED) in a separate proceeding, should be allowed to be operated by the party.Solicitor general Tushar Mehta, appearing for West Bengal govt, told a bench of Justices M M Sundresh and P B Varale that the accounts in question are frozen based on the FIR lodged by the state police, as there is evidence that Rs 35 crore, generated from the fraudulent sale of government land after it was misrepresented as private land by Abhishek Banerjee's PS Sumit Roy, was deposited in these bank accounts.Mehta also mentioned there is a plea pending before the EC as to which is the real TMC, the faction headed by Mamata or the rival group, adding that the EC has frozen the party symbol and allotted both factions ad hoc symbols to contest bypolls.The bench said it would not examine merits of the case as it is l pending with HC, which in the interim has already rejected the plea for de-freezing the accounts. It requested the HC to expedite adjudication of the pending petition on the issue.In its petition, the Mamata faction said it urgently required funds to meet expenses that would arise from preparations for the bypolls.Referring to an earlier ED proceeding freezing its three HDFC bank accounts, TMC said, "The FIR does not pertain to its Indian Bank accounts as no transaction is linked to the four bank accounts to the alleged offence.Successive and progressive freezing of TMC's bank accounts indicates mala fide use of power by state authorities to paralyse operations of a nationally recognised party."Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Virginia State University accused of suppressing Christian student ministries while Muslim groups are exempt
articles.summary: Alliance Defending Freedom sued Virginia State University over a policy allegedly forcing Christian student groups under a university-appointed minister.
articles.body: Virginia State University (VSU) is facing a federal lawsuit from two Christian student organizations that say the school stripped them of their official campus status and placed them under the direct authority of a university-appointed minister. "Higher education has really broke from its long-standing desire to promote intellectual diversity and to actually seek truth, and, instead, they are essentially telling students that any disagreement, that certain speech is violence and that hearing difference of opinions on important topics is actually not encouraged. It's actually discouraged," Alliance Defending Freedom (ADF) Senior Counsel Tyson Langhofer told Fox News Digital. "I think that higher education is really failing in its primary role, which is to educate the next generation … how to deal with living in a pluralistic society with people who have different opinions." 30% OF COLLEGE STUDENTS SAY VIOLENCE ACCEPTABLE WAY TO STOP SPEAKERS ON CAMPUSES, SURVEY FINDS Attorneys with ADF filed the lawsuit on behalf of campus chapters for Women of Victory and Bethel Campus Fellowship. The lawsuit challenges VSU’s updated Campus Ministries Policy, which plaintiffs argue violates the First Amendment by forcing Christian student groups under university control while granting exemptions to non-Christian religious groups. According to the policy, all Christian student-led ministries must operate under the "governance and influence" of VSU Campus Minister Thomas Wynn and an advisory board made up of faculty and university personnel. Additionally, the rule bans student ministries from affiliating with their national parent organizations. Langhofer told Fox News Digital the policy unconstitutionally penalizes Christian students for their religious beliefs. "The message that it would send is that the First Amendment means what it says: that you can't treat secular groups better than religious groups," Langhofer said. "You can't treat one religious group worse than another religious group, regardless of your motives. "It doesn't matter whether your motives are unity or things like that. You can't have one single campus pastor on campus that is able to control all Christian groups and then exclude the Muslim group and allow them to receive all of the benefits." GOP LAWMAKERS URGE SUPREME COURT TO STRENGTHEN FIRST AMENDMENT PROTECTIONS FOR STREET PREACHERS Non-Christian and Muslim student organizations remain exempt from the mandate, according to the legal filing. The lawsuit alleged that the policy targets Women of Victory and Bethel Campus Fellowship, both local chapters of national organizations that host Bible studies, leadership training and spiritual development events for students on and off campus. Although both groups remain listed on VSU’s official website, ADF representatives noted that the online directory does not reflect their current operational status on campus. The student organizations are seeking a court order restoring their status as fully recognized registered student organizations (RSOs). Langhofer pointed to "theological differences" between the campus pastor and the student organizations as a core issue created by the university's mandate. articles.title: The wealthy Cuban Americans ready and waiting for Havana to fall
articles.summary: Cuban exiles in Florida are increasingly hopeful that regime change in Cuba is now on the horizon.
articles.body:
At the lavish home of one of Miami's top plastic surgeons, overlooking the Biscayne Bay, some of the wealthiest Cuban-American families in Florida have gathered.

They are there to thrash out their vision of Cuba's future at the fourth meeting of the newly created Cuban-American National Chamber of Commerce (CANCC).

Rum in hand and Rolexes on wrists, this is Miami's old money. People with well-recognised Cuban-American surnames – like Bacardi and Babun – chat around the pool about the lamentable state of the island's economy, and share titbits of gossip about the latest political rumblings.

"The intention of this evening is to gather under one roof the most prominent Cuban-American entrepreneurs in Miami-Dade County," says CANCC president Juan Omar Sixto, "and the objective is to be in Cuba once the regime falls".

His guests are convinced that moment is nigh.

Millions without power as Cuba hit by latest major blackout

US sanctions more Cuban companies and officials

How the US oil blockade is pushing Cuba into darkness

This influential community of Cuban exiles has detested the Communist-run government ever since the late revolutionary leader Fidel Castro expropriated their lands and nationalised their families' companies after taking power in 1959.

And they have wielded their political and economic clout in Florida over the years to shape Washington's policies towards their homeland.

Sixto fled the island as a teenager. Now a real estate developer in his early 80s, his organisation is drafting plans for what he calls "the day after" in Cuba.

The CANCC has created a proposal for a Cuban Stock Exchange and formed committees on everything from energy infrastructure to food security.

Post-Communist planning is nothing new in Miami.

Countless documents and logistical plans have been drawn up by interest groups over the decades, some of them more sober and measured than others.

The difference now, insists Sixto, is the Trump administration's push to force total change on the island. And he says they have the ear of some high-profile contacts including people close to the Secretary of State, Marco Rubio.

"Together with deliveries of humanitarian aid and medical supplies, we'd go and do business in Cuba right away," says Sixto.

In Cuba itself, such claims are mostly met with scepticism.

In the face of Washington's "maximum pressure" campaign on Cuba, the island's leadership recently announced 176 economic liberalisation measures. The Cuban President, Miguel Díaz-Canel, said they were "to advance the defence of socialism, to support and widen social justice".

To his critics, they look distinctly like full-blown capitalism - lifting the cap on the number of workers in a private business, allowing the direct hiring and firing of Cuban employees and permitting ownership of multiple enterprises at once, including by Cuban Americans.

Still, the attendees at the CANCC meeting dismissed the economic reforms as cosmetic, saying they gave no meaningful guarantees to investors. They would "not put a foot into Cuba", Sixto said, while the current regime remained in place.

Some analysts think such planning meetings are premature. Although Cuban Americans are convinced that change is imminent in Cuba, none can say with any certainty what it will be - a US military operation as seen in Venezuela in January? Or a new economic pact with the island's leadership?

"Right now, the very high expectations created by the US administration that some kind of 'day after' was coming soon, or that Cuba would 'be next' have been kicked down the road," says Mike Bustamante, associate professor of history at the University of Miami.

With the November mid-term elections in the US approaching and the Trump administration embroiled in the "quagmire" of the Iran war, Bustamante argues there is little appetite for further foreign adventures.

"It's really tough to think that they will escalate further than what they're doing which is this drip-drip-drip of sanctions."

With the island's oil supply effectively shut off since January, that is already a significant escalation, says Mike Bustamente. Although they have made life unbearable for most ordinary people, they haven't yet "created the ingredients for a political inflection point" in Cuba, he adds.

The Cuban government has not commented on the CANCC itself. But traditionally such groups prompt indignation among revolutionaries who insist they will not be forced out by their critics in Miami.

I ask some guests if they can appreciate the irony that the same people who support a major source of the island's misery – the decades-long US economic embargo and the current fuel blockade – are now hatching plans for its reconstruction, without the input of most Cubans.

For Cuban-American agricultural expert Hugo Orizondo it is only practical to draw up a road map to Cuban development. "Right now, Cuba is like a black hole, we don't know what is happening over there," he admits. "But we do know the potential [for investment]."

Orizondo says he understands the reticence among Cubans to see foreign investors buying up something as sensitive as the rights to arable land. "But what are they going to do with it?" he retorts. "When investors come, they bring money and technology into the land."

Both are urgently needed, he says, if Cuba is ever to produce enough to feed its own population and break its reliance on food imports.

Land titles lie at the heart of any reconstruction project put forward by this generation of wealthy Cuban Americans. Juan Omar Sixto says his father lost five properties and a farm in Cuba's Pinar del Rio province to the revolution. While he insists he has no intention of removing any family living in those homes, he does want compensation for the nationalised land.

"I worked on that farm for five years of my life with my father, and they took it away. I want restitution or compensation. Even if they give me just a penny on the dollar, I'll take it."

The Cuban government portrays such historic title claims as bitterness by a corrupt landed gentry who made fortunes on the backs of indentured workers and slaves. Both slavery and the system of indentured workers didn't end in Cuba until the late 19th Century.

The government also argues that the exiles could never stand that Castro passed land reforms which handed over their fields to the workers and the state.

"Most of our sugar mills have been dismantled, but we will recover those lands and put them into production," says Nicolás Gutiérrez, the president of the National Association of Sugar Mill Owners of Cuba, an exile organisation championing the title claims.

"I'm not promising it will be in sugar," he says.

"It might be in ethanol, co-generation, solar panels or water purification cells. Who knows? There are a lot of different options," he remarks. "We need to get them producing, we need to have a real wage paid to Cuban workers and create a multiplier economic effect across the island."

With the ice clinking in their drinks and a cool breeze rustling the palm trees on the perfectly manicured lawn, the CANCC members make it sound easy. But within hours of their gathering, Cuba had descended into its sixth nationwide blackout this year.

The disconnection between the hopes for change in Miami and the realities on the ground in Cuba is stark. Many Miami-based Cubans think the monumental shift they have prayed for is almost here.

If so, it will inevitably bring huge social and humanitarian disruption which the stricken island is ill-equipped to cope with. Even assuming the diaspora's support is well-intentioned rather than purely self-interested, fixing the island's failing electrical grid alone is estimated to cost $8bn to $10bn (£6bn to £7.5bn).

Before any industry in Cuba – from agriculture to tourism – can be revitalised by the exiles' wealth and political connections, Cubans continue to face acute shortages in food, water, fuel and medicines. Miami's ambitious plans aside, most Cubans just hope their days get a little easier sometime soon.

articles.title: Why Gen Z are opting out of workplace pensions
articles.summary: A growing number of people are opting out of these schemes due to cost-of-living pressures.
articles.body:
Until early September, Hassan Nassar, 26, was saving around £430 every month into his NHS workplace pension.

But the trainee GP, who works in the West Midlands, says he was "really cash strapped" and decided to stop putting money aside for around "six to 12 months".

He needs the money to help take care of a sick family member, save for his first home and cover rent and student loan repayments.

But he's aware there is a cost to opting out, estimating he could lose between "£5,000 and £10,000" in future retirement income due to the decades of compound interest he will miss out on by not saving now.

"People will say, you're silly, look at what you'll be missing out in the future," he tells the BBC. "But I need to look at what I'd be losing now if I didn't opt out."

All employees will be automatically enrolled in a workplace pension if they are aged 22 or above and earn over £10,000, although there are exceptions.

A percentage is taken directly from the worker's pay - usually around 5% - with tax relief added on top, and the employer must also pay a minimum contribution on top.

But a growing number of Gen Z and millennials are opting out of these schemes due to cost-of-living pressures and the government has warned they could be on track for lower private pension incomes than people retiring today.

That is a problem, because while most people in the UK will eventually get a state pension , it only provides a minimum level of retirement income and many will rely on a private pension to supplement it.

Hassan says he was paying 10.7% of his gross earnings each month into his workplace pension, while the NHS contributed a substantial amount on top.

But unlike some employers, the NHS doesn't allow staff to reduce their contributions when times are hard.

Overall, however, he is confident he will have enough to retire on at the end of his "30-40" year career and is determined to opt back in to his pension as soon as he can.

According to the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP), around 22.6 million people, or 90% of those who are eligible for "automatic enrolment" pensions, are paying into one, while about 2.5 million are not.

However, Pensions Minister Torsten Bell told the BBC that "a rising number of young workers aren't saving, and overall there is a danger tomorrow's retirees are on track for lower private pension incomes than today's".

In the three months to December last year, 11.5% of eligible 22 to 29-year-olds who recently started a job opted out of their pensions. That's up from 6.6% in the same period of 2020.

For 30 to 39-year-olds it's gone from 7.4% to 12.7%.

Evie, 22, from Cornwall, says she opted out of entering the workplace pension at the London events company she works for.

A recent drama school graduate, she says she would have struggled to cover her outgoings, including food, travel and the £800 she pays in rent.

Evie is conscious about missing out on saving for retirement, but there are other things she needs money for that make it impractical right now.

"How can I save for a house, how can I save for a car and afford my outgoings? I don't want to just work day in, day out to live, I want to work to have a life."

April Leeson, from The Private Office, a chartered financial advice firm, says she would always advise people to not stop paying into their pensions if they can help it, even if that means reducing their contributions, which many employers allow you to do.

This is partly because of the free employer contributions they will miss out on but also the lost compound interest.

"The current minimum pension age is 57, so any money you save in your 20s will have at least 30 years to compound and grow.

"£100 saved now, compounded at 4% a year over 30 years, is going to be worth a lot more than £100 saved in 15 to 20 years' time."

She also urges younger people to think ahead. "You really need to think of your future self and what that person will need to retire comfortably."

Kharlee, 47, a teacher from South East London, can certainly relate to this. She stopped her contributions to a workplace pension twice over the last five years for financial reasons.

And she thinks she missed out on saving about £5,000 into her pension pot.

She's in a better place financially now, but recently became self-employed and is no longer part of a private pension scheme, something she hopes to change.

"I would like to feel my pension is secure, and I don't feel like that. I worry I'm not going to be able to live comfortably at the age of retirement."

articles.title: At Washington’s tomb, a British royal honors the man who kicked out the Crown
articles.summary: Britain’s Prince Edward followed his Great Great Grandfather’s tradition by laying a wreath at the tomb of Washington at his Mount Vernon home.
articles.body: On an autumn day in 1860, a bearded British man visited George Washington’s tomb at his final resting place in Virginia. While there he paused to plant a small buckeye tree. The tree would grow, and so would he, to become King Edward VII of England, King of the United Kingdom and the British Dominions, Emperor of India. During that humble pilgrimage, the then Prince Albert Edward, began a long tradition of members of the British royal family visiting George Washington’s Mount Vernon, a sort of reverent homage to the man who helped end British rule, and set a rot in the Empire. Over 160 years later, on a particularly warm October day the modern Prince Edward followed his Great Great Grandfather’s tradition by laying a wreath at the tomb of Washington at his Mount Vernon home. History was repeating, ancient bonds once damaged in war, silenced, and soothed in the quiet moments after. A group of tourists at Mount Vernon told the duke and the cluster of those associated with with Mount Vernon, that they had come from all over North America to share the moment, and themselves remake bonds broken some two and half centuries ago. The duke is the second senior royal to go on a pilgrimage to America this year as it celebrates its 250th birthday. In part it is a reaffirmation of America’s independence by a family who felt its less-than-harmonious divorce from British rule more than any other, and a celebration of the bonds that now exist. When King Charles III made his first visit as monarch to Washington DC earlier this year, he and US President Donald Trump highlighted the importance of the enduring “special relationship” between the US and the UK. “Ours is a partnership born out of dispute, but no less strong for it, so perhaps, in this example, we can discern that our nations are in fact instinctively like-minded – a product of the common democratic, legal and social traditions in which our governance is rooted to this day,” the king said his speech to Congress this year. During the duke’s visit to Virginia that “special relationship” returned to center stage. This week as a UK airbase used by the US military appeared under serious threat, Trump sang his special partner’s praises in partnering to hunt down the assumed attackers, saying the US was “working with Britain, it was an amazing job.” However, Trump’s announcement last week that he might ban diesel exports, including to the UK — which imports one third of its diesel from the US — became a bit of a buzz kill on the base cooperation vibe. Diesel prices on UK forecourts are the highest they’ve ever been, economists are raising the alarm and the oh-so-elusive special bond is yo-yoing toward breaking point. Christian Turner, the United Kingdom’s Ambassador to the US, who accompanied the duke as he walked in his long-dead relative’s footsteps, told CNN that these types of government issues do not affect royal visits. “As his Majesty the King said in his address to Congress it’s really a moment to step up and back and remind us that the relationship is bigger than an ambassador, a president, a duke, a secretary of state, and it’s those ties and those connections that stretch back in history and stretch forward,” the ambassador said. “It’s true, constitutionally, for us the monarchy is above politics so we’re not discussing day to day policy on trips like this, we’re thinking about those deeper ties and why still, after 250 years, we’re family.” As the prince and escorts paused to enjoy a farewell stop at the Mount Vernon Whiskey tasting, there was another subtle reminder that no matter how special the bond, even shared histories lead to different places. In this case, the spelling of the word, “Whiskey,” which in the UK is spelt with an “e” if it comes from Ireland and no “e” if it comes from Scotland. “Technically it’s either Scottish or Irish, so you’re going to have to try and work out whether you’re going to have to spell it differently to indicate it’s over here,” the duke mused. “You could replace the ‘I’ with a ‘u’,” he quipped.

articles.title: What's really going on in lymphatic drainage beauty trend videos?
articles.summary: Fans of these massages claim they "depuff" and "define" their stomach - but what's actually happening to their bodies?
articles.body:
If she's ever feeling bloated, Abbey Alexandra has a go-to routine, using body oil and a wooden roller to perform stomach massages.

She shares before-and-after videos on TikTok, saying she feels the process leaves her depuffed and defined: "You definitely feel a lot better after, they are relaxing."

The technique is a form of lymphatic drainage massage, adapted from a medical treatment and shared as a beauty trend. Celebrity fans include Maya Jama, who shares her clinic sessions, and actress Hailey Bieber, who told Time magazine: "I swear by them."

Whether there is a physical change - or any need for one - is debatable, but fans of the massages claim they help "flatten" and "debloat" and give a "snatched waist" and "sculpted abs". But what's actually happening to their bodies?

Many videos on social media promoting lymphatic massage show a woman either standing sideways, facing the front or perhaps lying down with her stomach showing a slight - and very normal - curve outwards.

Then begins the methodical massage in circular motions seemingly draining fluid away. By the end, her stomach appears flatter - if a little red.

But social media body trends should always be viewed with scepticism, says Dr Ella Guest, senior research fellow and health psychologist at the Centre for Appearance Research based at the University of the West of England.

"These images might be altered using photo-editing tools or filters, people standing in particular poses, use of lighting, lots could even be AI-generated," she says.

"I think stopping to reflect on what you see and questioning whether it looks realistic, or if it's very aligned with beauty standards, can be useful. Remember, if something looks too good to be true, it probably is."

The lymphatic system is a network of channels and glands throughout the body that helps fight infection and remove excess fluid, according to the NHS.

Dr Xand van Tulleken tells Morning Live that the lymphatic system helps remove excess fluid from tissues and supports the immune system.

"When it is not working properly, it can contribute to swelling, which can be a condition called lymphoedema."

This commonly affects people who have cancers that involve the lymph system or who've had treatment involving the lymph nodes.

It causes swelling in any part of the body, but usually develops in the arms or legs.

"In simple terms, the lymphatic system helps keep your body's fluid levels balanced, cleans up waste, and supports your defences against illness," says van Tulleken.

Dr Xand says manual lymphatic drainage is one of a range of treatments used by medical professionals "if your lymphatic system isn't working as it should".

He describes it as using "light pressure" and "strategic massage techniques" to "clear" your lymphatic system.

"They'll coax excess lymph fluid from your swollen tissues toward your lymph nodes, where the lymph can reabsorb," he says - adding lymph nodes are found in the armpits, neck and groin.

He adds that these massages can be a "safe way" to relieve symptoms for conditions like lymphoedema but are not suitable for some people with pre-existing medical conditions.

He stresses: "No one should get their health advice from Instagram - far safer to use the NHS website, or consult your GP."

Abbey, who has endometriosis which she says causes her to feel bloated, began doing her own massage routines twice a week aer seeing social media posts about lymphatic drainage.

"I started using my hands and then I bought some wooden tools as well.

"After doing my routine, I personally feel less puffy and bloated, particularly around my stomach.

"Visually, I notice that my stomach looks a little more defined and I also feel lighter and more comfortable."

Dr Xand says there is "no need" for most people to perform lymphatic drainage treatments at home.

"There is very little high-quality evidence showing they provide meaningful or lasting benefits for healthy individuals, and it does not promote fat loss," he says.

But he does note that lymphatic drainage massages can feel "relaxing" and some people "can notice a temporary reduction in swelling".

"For most healthy people, regular movement, exercise and staying hydrated are all that's needed to support normal lymphatic function," he says.

"Unless someone has a diagnosed lymphatic condition, I don't think anyone needs routine lymphatic drainage treatments, despite the growing popularity of these practices on social media."

For Abbey, it's something she enjoys. "I know the visual difference is temporary... But I do like how I look and feel afterwards so it'll always be a part of my routine."

However, Guest warns striving for a sculpted stomach could "feed into people's insecurities".

"We know that when we compare ourselves online and try to live up to these trends, we tend to scrutinise our appearance more and feel less satisfied with how we look," she says.

"The reality is that healthy bodies come in a wide range of shapes and sizes."
